entry.title: A Critical Look at Power Sampling when Test Time Sharpening LLMs

link.title: A Critical Look at Power Sampling when Test Time Sharpening LLMs

entry.content:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved LLM reasoning, yet growing evidence suggests it mainly performs distribution sharpening: concentrating probability mass on reasoning paths the base model already produces. Recent work therefore seeks RLVR’s gains without needing reward signals, by sampling from the power distribution $\pi_\alpha \propto \pi_{\text{base}}^\alpha$ via Markov chain Monte Carlo or sequential Monte Carlo. We show that these samplers fail to converge to $\pi_\alpha$ under realistic compute budgets, and that their gains are largely recreated via simple Best-of-$N$ with appropriate grading . This suggests they succeed by selecting high-probability sequences, not by approximating $\pi_\alpha$, raising a natural question: is the power distribution itself a worthwhile target? We test this hypothesis directly by fine-tuning the base model to match $\pi_\alpha$, sidestepping sampler convergence issues entirely. Despite approximating the target far more faithfully than existing samplers, this strategy yields gains that are noisy and specific to certain models and sampling tasks. Together, our results suggest that the value of power sampling lies not in faithfully targeting $\pi_\alpha$, but in the simpler goal of extracting sequences the base model already deems likely.

entry.title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models

link.title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models

entry.content:
Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.

entry.title: A Moment-assisted Approach for Improving Subsampling-based MLE with Large-scale data

link.title: A Moment-assisted Approach for Improving Subsampling-based MLE with Large-scale data

entry.content:
The maximum likelihood estimation is computationally demanding for large datasets, particularly when the likelihood function includes integrals. Subsampling can reduce the computational burden, but it often results in efficiency loss.This paper proposes a moment-assisted subsampling (MAS) method that can improve the estimation efficiency of existing subsampling-based maximum likelihood estimators.The motivation behind this approach stems from the fact that sample moments can be efficiently computed even if the sample size of the whole data set is huge.Through the generalized method of moments, the proposed method incorporates informative sample moments of the whole data. The MAS estimator can be computed rapidly and is asymptotically normal with a smaller asymptotic variance than the corresponding estimator without incorporating sample moments of the whole data. The asymptotic variance of the proposed estimator depends on the specific sample moments incorporated. We derive the optimal moment that minimizes the resulting asymptotic variance in terms of Loewner order. The proposed MAS estimator can achieve the same estimation efficiency as the whole data-based estimator when the optimal moment is incorporated. Numerical results demonstrate the promising performance of the proposed method in both estimation and computational efficiency compared with existing subsampling methods.

entry.title: A Theory of the Mechanics of Information: Generalization Through Measurement of Uncertainty (Learning is Measuring)

link.title: A Theory of the Mechanics of Information: Generalization Through Measurement of Uncertainty (Learning is Measuring)

entry.content:
Traditional machine learning relies on explicit models and domain assumptions, often limiting flexibility and interpretability. We introduce a “model-free” framework of instance-based learning using surprisal (information theoretic uncertainty) to directly analyze and perform inferences from raw data, eliminating distribution modeling, reducing bias, and enabling efficient updates including direct edits and deletion of training data. By quantifying relevance through uncertainty, the approach enables generalizable inference across tasks including generative inference, causal discovery, anomaly detection, and time series forecasting. Our approach emphasizes traceability, interpretability, and data-driven decision making, offering a unified, human-understandable framework for machine learning, can be adapted to virtually all machine learning tasks, achieving competency across all and state-of-the-art performance on anomaly detection and some supervised tasks. The mathematical foundations create a “physics” of information, which enable these techniques to apply effectively to a wide variety of complex data types, including missing data. Our results suggest that this may be a viable foundation upon which to build scalable machine learning and artificial intelligence that can maintain human understandability of the underlying mechanics.

entry.title: Active Sequential Signal Detection with Asynchronous Decisions

link.title: Active Sequential Signal Detection with Asynchronous Decisions

entry.content:
The problem of quickly detecting signals among multiple sequentially observed data streams, subject to constraints on the familywise false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities, is considered under an active sampling setup where only one stream can be sampled at each time instant. Under this setup, it is in general impossible to minimize, even asymptotically, the expected decision time simultaneously for every stream. We therefore consider minimizing the expected time until either the kth signal declaration or termination simultaneously for every k. We first establish non-asymptotic lower bounds for these criteria. For k > B , where B denotes the true subset of signals, we show that these lower bounds are attained asymptotically as the error levels vanish by any policy that stops sampling and makes a decision for each stream according to a local Sequential Probability Ratio Test. For 1 <= k <= B , however, the performance depends critically on the sampling rule, and we propose one with a simple exploration mechanism that prevents switching away from signals prematurely because of early unfavorable observations. We show that, under a mild relative-rate condition on the two error levels, the resulting policy attains all the lower bounds simultaneously. Numerical studies are presented to compare the proposed policy with an oracle policy and a follow-the-leader policy.

entry.title: A functional mixed-effects model for the joint analysis of amplitude and phase variations in function-valued traits

link.title: A functional mixed-effects model for the joint analysis of amplitude and phase variations in function-valued traits

entry.content:
Quantitative genetics is the study of continuous traits and the statistical analysis of phenotypic variation, that is, the observable differences in physical traits among individuals within a population. If family relationships between individuals are known, phenotypic variation can be partitioned into genetic and environmental components. Some traits, such as growth trajectories, can be described as a function of a continuous index and are known as function-valued traits. However, function-valued traits from different individuals often vary not only in their shape (amplitude) but also in the speed at which the biological process develops (phase). In this work, we present and compare two approaches to account for amplitude and phase variations in estimating the additive genetic and environmental components. The first one follows from a conventional framework where warping functions remove phase variations, and then the aligned curves are analysed. The second approach adopts the perspective of looking at the aligned curve and the warping function as a joint functional object. In both cases, we propose a functional mixed-effects framework that uses functional principal components as the data-driven basis for genetically correlated data. The proposed procedure is applied to simulations and a real-case study of Tribolium castaneum growth trajectories.

entry.title: Amortised Inference through One-Step Implicit Sampling

link.title: Amortised Inference through One-Step Implicit Sampling

entry.content:
Efficient sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions in high dimensions remains a hard problem, despite advances in theory and algorithms. Multiple steps are usually required to draw unbiased samples, for example, iterations of an MCMC algorithm or integration steps in a diffusion-based amortised sampler. However, scalable one-step amortised inference remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we build upon recent progress in data-driven generative modelling to offer a possible solution for one-step amortised sampling. Our one-step implicit sampler (OSIS) uses short-time MCMC dynamics to define a local target for the evolution of an implicitly modelled distribution. In the asymptotic limit, the modelled distribution is a fixed point of the MCMC kernel and thus samples from the target. We analyse the convergence properties of OSIS and show connections with other generative modelling and sampling algorithms. We study various design choices and show that OSIS performs well compared to multi-step amortised samplers and non-amortised MCMC baselines while being far more efficient at sampling time.

entry.title: An efficient stochastic generalized method of moments estimator for nonlinear moment models

link.title: An efficient stochastic generalized method of moments estimator for nonlinear moment models

entry.content:
We study the asymptotic properties of the nonlinear stochastic GMM algorithm proposed by Chen, Lee, Liao, Seo, Shin and Song for recursively estimating parameters defined by possibly nonlinear and overidentified moment restrictions $\E[g(X,\beta^*)]=0$. Each observation updates estimates of the moment Jacobian, inverse covariance matrix and Gauss–Newton preconditioner at a cost independent of sample size. For linear and nonlinear instrumental-variable moments, we derive an exact rank-two Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury update. The algorithm combines preconditioned stochastic approximation with iterate averaging. Under a preconditioned monotonicity condition, satisfied globally in linear models and locally around a consistent pilot estimate in general, we establish almost sure convergence and rates, as well as a functional central limit theorem with the efficient GMM variance. These results require four moments of the moment function and its Jacobian when the step exponent exceeds $2/3$. The inverse Gauss–Newton matrix consistently estimates this variance, and a projected linearised statistic enables online testing of overidentifying restrictions. We extend the results to $L$-dependent data with long-run variance weights under stronger moment assumptions. Simulations show that the averaged estimator approaches offline two-step GMM in accuracy and coverage at $10^6$ observations, while requiring a fraction of its computing time and fixed memory at up to $10^7$ observations. The online test achieves correct size and comparable power. In an application estimating the effect of a third child on weeks worked using $254{,}654$ women from the 1980 US Census, single-pass estimates agree with offline GMM within a fraction of a standard error on average across data orderings, and both methods yield the same overidentification-test conclusion in most orderings.

entry.title: Approximation of differential entropy in Bayesian optimal experimental design

link.title: Approximation of differential entropy in Bayesian optimal experimental design

entry.content:
Bayesian optimal experimental design provides a principled framework for selecting experimental configurations that maximize obtained information. In this work, we consider settings where the likelihood entropy is independent of the design or can be evaluated explicitly, which applies, e.g. to additive noise models with design-independent or explicitly computable noise entropy. This reduces the problem to maximum entropy estimation, where the nested integral defining the expected information gain collapses into a single integral. Our study is motivated by large-scale inference problems, such as inverse problems, where the computational cost is dominated by expensive likelihood evaluations. Under additive Gaussian noise model, we propose a computational approach in which the evidence density is approximated by a Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo surrogate, while the differential entropy is evaluated using standard methods without additional likelihood evaluations. We prove that this strategy achieves convergence rates that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods for full expected information gain estimation, particularly when the cost of entropy evaluation is negligible. Our approach relies only on mild smoothness of the forward map and avoids stronger technical assumptions required in earlier work. We also present numerical experiments, which confirm some of our theoretical findings.

entry.title: Arctan-skewing: a new skewing scheme on the hypertorus

link.title: Arctan-skewing: a new skewing scheme on the hypertorus

entry.content:
In this paper we propose and study arctan-skewing, a general approach to skew any symmetric distribution on the unit hypertorus. Arctan-skewing retains the main advantages of the popular sine-skewing mechanism, but improves on it by overcoming its two major limitations. These are a condition on the skewness parameter and a singular Fisher Information matrix in the vicinity of symmetry when combined with well-known symmetric models from the literature such as the circular von Mises or bivariate Cosine models. Arctan-skewing thus represents a compelling alternative to model skewed data on the circle and torus, notably from the field of protein bioinformatics. After a thorough investigation of its stochastic properties, we present a maximum likelihood estimation procedure and devise optimal tests for symmetry against our new class of skewed alternatives. Finally we show that arctan-skewed models better fit protein data compared to their sine-skewed counterparts.

entry.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning

link.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning

entry.content:
Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nystr"om-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.

entry.title: Bayesian dynamic scheduling of multipurpose batch processes under incomplete look-ahead information

link.title: Bayesian dynamic scheduling of multipurpose batch processes under incomplete look-ahead information

entry.content:
Multipurpose batch processes become increasingly popular in manufacturing industries since they adapt to low-volume, high-value products and shifting demands. These processes often operate in a dynamic environment, which faces disturbances such as processing delays and demand changes. To minimise long-term cost and system nervousness (i.e., disruptive changes to schedules), schedulers must design rescheduling strategies to address such disturbances effectively. Existing methods often assume complete look-ahead information over the scheduling horizon. This assumption contrasts with realistic situations where schedulers can only access incomplete look-ahead information. Sticking with existing methods may lead to suboptimal long-term costs and high-level system nervousness. In this work we propose a Bayesian dynamic scheduling method. Our method relies on learning a Bayesian Network from the probability distribution of disturbances. Specifically, the Bayesian Network represents how likely each operation will be impacted by disturbances. During the online execution, when new disturbances become observed, this method updates the posterior distribution and therefore guides the rescheduling strategy. We compare our method with the existing periodic rescheduling strategy (which generates new schedules from scratch at fixed intervals) on four benchmark problems. Computational results show that our method achieves statistically better long-term costs and system nervousness. In the theoretical aspect, we prove that if disturbances are mutually independent, the impact-quantifying variables inherently satisfy the independence assumptions required by Bayesian Networks. As an implication, practitioners can extend the method to other scheduling problems (such as job shop scheduling and continuous processes), given that they define the problem-specific dependencies between operations.

entry.title: Beyond Discrepancy: Oracle Drift in Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization

link.title: Beyond Discrepancy: Oracle Drift in Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization

entry.content:
We analyze distributional drift in nonstationary weighted risk minimization by decomposing the excess risk into estimation, drift, and approximation components. The drift error is commonly bounded through discrepancy-type quantities that control changes of the risk over classes of predictors. We instead relate the drift error directly to the movement of the best predictor within the model class and analyze its behavior in parametrized regression models. Our analysis shows that discrepancy-type quantities can be overly conservative: unlike our oracle drift, they may scale at a larger order than the resulting excess-risk contribution and can respond to changes in the risk surface that do not affect the optimal predictor. For linear regression, we characterize this gap sharply and combine the resulting drift bounds with estimation guarantees. We further extend the analysis to nonparametric regression.

entry.title: Beyond Second-Order Information: Paid Logistic Regression with Noisy Features

link.title: Beyond Second-Order Information: Paid Logistic Regression with Noisy Features

entry.content:
We consider online binary prediction with paid stochastic features, where the learner can spend resources to obtain better observations of the underlying features. This setting is motivated by applications such as medical testing, where additional cost can provide more precise measurements of patient’s features for predicting a binary outcome. At each round, a latent feature is drawn i.i.d., the response is generated through a logistic model, and the learner chooses how much to pay before observing a noisy version of the feature. The goal of learner is to jointly control prediction loss and acquisition cost. In contrast to the former result on the online linear regression with paid features, covariance information alone is no longer sufficient: two noise distributions with the same covariance may induce different optimal logistic losses, and lower variance can even lead to higher loss. Under a structural ordering in which larger payments yield better observations by removing independent noise, we obtain $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ regret when the noise structure is known and $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ regret when it is unknown, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks

link.title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks

entry.content:
Neural networks (NNs), while highly flexible and versatile, are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration methods adjust the outputs of an already trained model using a separate calibration dataset and additional calibration parameters. This process adds overhead that requires separate optimization of the calibrator and subsequent model selection. In this paper, we show that standard (post-hoc) calibrators can be trained end-to-end with the backbone via a bilevel Stackelberg formulation. This formulation eliminates the need for a separate calibration set or a dedicated calibration loss by jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration using cross-entropy, introducing only one additional hyperparameter: the calibrator learning rate. Although our framework supports calibrators ranging from temperature and matrix scaling to NN layers, our results show that using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no additional parameters. Our approach outperforms SOTA calibrators with minimal added complexity, while also avoiding the multiplicative overhead of separate calibration components in settings such as multi-task learning.

entry.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO

link.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO

entry.content:
Estimating the first stage of an instrumental variables (IV) model with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary of technical instruments and a penalty level. First-order asymptotic theory offers no guidance on these choices, as any consistent implementation yields a structural parameter estimator with the same limiting distribution. In finite samples, however, these choices can have a substantial impact on the resulting structural parameter estimate. Working in a model with a single endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors, we use first- and second-order Stein identities to derive the approximate mean squared error (AMSE) of the instrumental-variables LASSO (IV-LASSO) estimator, which can be consistently estimated and used to rank a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty candidates. The AMSE reveals a bias-variance trade-off: more complex first-stage fits better approximate the conditional mean of the endogenous variable but are also more correlated with the structural errors, with complexity measured by the degrees of freedom of the LASSO fit. The weight on this bias rises with the endogeneity of the regressor, a quantity that neither plug-in nor cross-validation penalty rules take into account. Despite the AMSE being derived in a Gaussian model, penalty selection by minimizing the feasible AMSE criterion delivers up to a one-third lower mean squared error compared to cross-validation and plug-in penalty rules in Gaussian and non-Gaussian simulation designs calibrated to the data of Gilchrist and Sands (2016).

entry.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning

link.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning

entry.content:
Bayes’ theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.

entry.title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints

link.title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints

entry.content:
Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors rather than point estimates, but they condition only on equality information: the PDE residual, boundary data, and measurements. Many solutions of interest also obey inequality constraints, including nonnegativity, monotonicity, and absence of arbitrage, which equality conditioning cannot enforce. We prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite-dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially in terms of Borel measures on the solution space. The physics-informed posterior is therefore a valid prior for the inequality update at virtual points. The combined law is non-Gaussian yet computable through truncated-Gaussian moments, and neither the PDE conditioning nor the inequality update requires modification. We evaluated the construction on a Poisson benchmark, option-price surfaces, and air-quality fields. Under incomplete boundary data, a monotonicity constraint lowered the error of a two-dimensional Poisson reconstruction by $63\%$. On a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to $20$ retained quotes, no-arbitrage constraints reduced held-out extrapolation error by $22\%$ and cut the calendar-arbitrage rate from $10\%$ to $1\%$. On four real air-quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a Gaussian moment-based sub-zero-tail proxy by $74\%$ at the sparsest monitor count. Changes in mean accuracy and constraint diagnostics differed across data regimes. The probability of the noisy virtual constraint event under the equality posterior measures agreement with the specified bounds before the update. The construction turns admissibility from a post-processing step into conditioning information for probabilistic PDE solvers.

entry.title: CorrFlow: Exact and Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching on the Correlation Elliptope

link.title: CorrFlow: Exact and Permutation-Equivariant Flow Matching on the Correlation Elliptope

entry.content:
Correlation matrices combine nonlinear positive-definiteness constraints with a simultaneous row-column permutation symmetry. Their generation therefore involves two distinct problems. First, every output must remain on the correlation elliptope, irrespective of how its variables are ordered. Second, the generator must learn the domain-specific distribution occupied by empirical data inside that valid space. Existing financial image generators mix these problems: they learn ordered matrix entries and repair invalid draws afterward. We introduce CorrFlow, which separates them. A generalized Fisher transform maps full-rank correlation matrices bijectively to unconstrained coordinates, guaranteeing valid outputs without projection. A graph flow-matching network learns the empirical distribution in those coordinates and is permutation equivariant: reordering the variables only reorders the output. We compare a conditional CorrGAN reimplementation, image diffusion, and CorrFlow on $80\times80$ Taiwan equity matrices using five seeds per neural method. CorrFlow produces 100% valid draws without repair and obtains feature sliced-Wasserstein distance $.712\pm.141$, versus $4.339\pm.252$ for CorrGAN and $4.610\pm.191$ for image diffusion after their invalid outputs are projected back to the correlation space. It also improves this distance over historical lookup, while lookup retains higher local coverage. These results support the combined construction under the evaluated training budget; they do not establish superiority over fully tuned image models or isolate the contribution of each component.

entry.title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes

link.title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes

entry.content:
The two main traditional player statistics used in soccer are goals scored and assists, with an assist credited when a player’s pass immediately leads to a teammate scoring. Attributing credit solely to the player who makes the final pass before a goal fails to account for the contributions of multiple players in the buildup to the goal. Consequently, traditional statistics provide only a limited view of player involvement. In this paper, we use multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) to model timestamped sequences of passes and shots, which form continuous-time networks. MHPs provide a branching mechanism where an event (a pass or shot) can be generated as a child of a previous event, which allows us to quantify each pass’s contribution to a subsequent pass or shot. This approach distributes credit across multiple passes within an attacking sequence, making it applicable across a wide range of situations. Building on this framework, we propose expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that measures a player’s involvement in creating goal scoring opportunities based on their passes. This metric identifies players who play key roles in creating goal scoring opportunities even if they do not make the final pass, offering a more comprehensive measure of attacking involvement and player performance.

entry.title: Data-Driven Stochastic Optimal Control in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

link.title: Data-Driven Stochastic Optimal Control in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

entry.content:
This paper proposes a fully data-driven approach for optimal control of nonlinear control-affine systems represented by a stochastic diffusion. The focus is on the scenario where both the nonlinear dynamics and stage cost functions are unknown, while only a control penalty function and constraints are provided. To this end, we embed state probability densities into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) to leverage recent advances in operator regression, thereby identifying Markov transition operators associated with controlled diffusion processes. This operator learning approach integrates naturally with convex operator-theoretic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman recursions that scale linearly with state dimensionality, effectively solving a wide range of nonlinear optimal control problems. Numerical results demonstrate its ability to address diverse nonlinear control tasks, including the depth regulation of an autonomous underwater vehicle.

entry.title: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning

link.title: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning

entry.content:
When a language model is distilled from a teacher that shares its base parameters, the student can inherit behavioural traits of the teacher—including misalignment—even from data that is semantically unrelated to the trait (Cloud et al., 2026). All existing defences require knowing the trait. We remove this requirement and prove that a subliminally transferred trait can be recovered from the parameter updates alone, without supervision, by exploiting a single asymmetry: the trait is expressed consistently across diverse datasets generated by the teacher, whereas task-specific and shared capabilities vary. The resulting estimator returns a weight-space direction that can be amplified to discover and interpret the trait or projected out to suppress it. Applied to the subliminal-learning benchmarks of (Cloud et al., 2026), our method recovers the transmitted animal-preference traits without any trait labels and suppresses their expression with almost no impact to task performance.

entry.title: Design-based effect sizes and their synthesis in randomized multiple-baseline experiments

link.title: Design-based effect sizes and their synthesis in randomized multiple-baseline experiments

entry.content:
Effect sizes for single-case experimental designs usually rely on models for the baseline trend and the serial dependence, which are challenging to check with few sessions. We develop design-based effect sizes for multiple-baseline experiments with a randomized intervention onset. We define case-level and pooled standardized effects with potential outcomes and propose weighted estimators that are unbiased or asymptotically unbiased without an outcome model. The usual difference between phase means is generally biased when the untreated outcome changes over sessions. For research synthesis, we provide variance estimators and asymptotic confidence intervals that require no model for serial dependence, and variance formulas for planning. Simulations and three randomized studies of reading and writing interventions illustrate the methods.

entry.title: Disentangling Total-Variance and Signal-to-Noise-Ratio Improves Diffusion Models

link.title: Disentangling Total-Variance and Signal-to-Noise-Ratio Improves Diffusion Models

entry.content:
Diffusion models have been widely adopted as a powerful generative framework across numerous scientific domains, yet their inherently iterative sampling process remains a significant computational bottleneck. While this is typically mitigated by reducing the number of reverse diffusion steps, sample quality becomes highly sensitive to the chosen noise schedule, i.e. the manner in which noise is introduced and the signal is reduced at each step. Although prior work has improved on the original variance-preserving and variance-exploding schedules, these approaches passively adjust the total variance, without direct independent control over it. In this work, we propose a novel total-variance/signal-to-noise-ratio disentangled (TV/SNR) framework, where TV and SNR can be controlled independently. Our approach reveals that schedules with exponentially exploding TV can be consistently improved by adopting a constant TV schedule while preserving the underlying SNR schedule. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalizing the SNR schedule of optimal transport flow matching significantly enhances generation efficiency. Crucially, these gains remain consistent across various reverse diffusion solvers and reduce the search space to two independent and interpretable parameters, enabling fast and robust sampling for complex scientific applications, such as molecular structure generation.

entry.title: Enhancing credit risk scorecards with transactional-based behavioural features

link.title: Enhancing credit risk scorecards with transactional-based behavioural features

entry.content:
Background: Credit risk modelling is fundamental in financial institutions, typically using credit history, repayment behaviour, income, and outstanding debt to estimate a borrower’s probability of default. Although transactional data are sometimes incorporated through aggregated measures such as recency, frequency, and monetary indicators, behavioural information embedded in raw transaction narratives remains largely unexplored due to its unstructured nature. This limits opportunities to extract richer behavioural insights. Aim: This research investigates payment narratives from transactional data as an alternative data source for credit risk modelling. Setting: The study uses transactional data from a large South African financial institution focused on small and medium enterprises. Method: Techniques such as natural language processing and regular expressions are used to transform unstructured transaction descriptions into meaningful, explainable behavioural features by categorising transactions into interpretable spending categories. A novel categorisation algorithm was developed and evaluated for classification accuracy. The extracted features are incorporated into a credit risk scorecard to assess their predictive value. Results: The categorisation algorithm demonstrates high classification accuracy. Using these features in the scorecard resulted in a significant increase in Gini compared to a scorecard without them. Conclusion: Text-based transactional information can be systematically extracted, categorised, and operationalised to enhance credit risk model performance. Contribution: The study develops a novel, integrated, explainable methodology for transforming transactional text into behavioural features, introduces a structured RegEx-based categorisation approach, and demonstrates their predictive value within traditional scorecard frameworks.

link.title: Estimating Great Expectations Under Autoregressive Language Models with Potentials

entry.content:
Many applications of language models hinge not on individual samples but on the expectation of a test functional under the model. Estimating such expectations reliably can be computationally expensive. We do so through potentials: real-valued functions on prefixes that decompose the test functional additively. We construct an estimator whose variance depends on the chosen potential, and derive conditions under which a potential reduces this variance. We then develop practical potentials for several estimands and applications, and demonstrate substantial variance reductions across several estimands at comparable computational cost.

We present a simulation-based method for the estimation, sensitivity analysis, and optimization of distortion risk measures (DRMs), a class of performance measures that capture a wide range of risk attitudes through an underlying distortion function. Under suitable conditions, we establish strong consistency and convergence rates for DRM estimation, sensitivity analysis, and optimization. We further extend the approach to non-polynomial distortion functions through polynomial approximation. entry.title: Explicit Asymptotic Bounds for Sequential Calibration Beyond $T^{2/3}$

link.title: Explicit Asymptotic Bounds for Sequential Calibration Beyond $T^{2/3}$

entry.content:
Probability forecasts are calibrated when predicted probabilities match empirical outcome frequencies: among events assigned a probability $p$, we’d hope that the fraction of positive outcomes is close to $p$. We study the problem of sequential forecasting of binary outcomes. The classical $O(T^{2/3})$ bound on expected cumulative $\ell_1$-calibration error established by Foster and Vohra stood for over two decades until Dagan et al. reduced the exponent $2/3$ by an unspecified constant. We establish a new two-phase recursive labeling strategy for the sign-preservation-with-reuse game that yields the bound $O(n^{\alpha}t^\beta)$ for all choices of space and time. We then sharpen the reduction from upper bounds on sign preservation to calibration by modifying the equivalence of Dagan et al. to use only $O(\log T)$ instances of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game. This lets us establish an explicit bound of $O(T^{0.662942288})$, the first explicit exponent below $2/3$ for sequential calibration, by combining both improvements and choosing explicit feasible parameters.

entry.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance

link.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance

entry.content:
Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tools have often been presented as methods to increase trust in machine learning models by making aspects of their algorithms more human-understandable. However, evidence accumulated over the last decade points to an overall failure of this objective, instead promoting overreliance on incorrect predictions, which can subsequently lead to algorithmic aversion. Rather, XAI appears to function primarily as a debugging tool, useful for obtaining anecdotal insights into, for example, features learned by the model. One of the main issues underlying this limitation is that XAI methods often oversimplify the inner workings of the model, resulting in misalignment between the explanation and the model itself - a behavior referred to as unfaithfulness or infidelity. Faithfulness can be interpreted as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model. Computing faithfulness in a rigorous manner would thus make it possible to quantify one of the various elements of trustworthiness of an explanation. However, existing metrics present significant limitations, making this quantification either infeasible or computationally expensive. In this position paper, we outline five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics and propose four possible avenues for research to bolster their reliability.

entry.title: Fast Gradient-Based Approximation of Continuous Dynamic Time Warping

link.title: Fast Gradient-Based Approximation of Continuous Dynamic Time Warping

entry.content:
Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a common choice for measuring the discrepancy between time series. It proceeds by finding an optimal warping between timestamps through dynamic programming, which can be slow and is not differentiable. Consequently, several variants have been proposed. Among them, Soft-DTW proposes a smooth formulation of DTW, amenable to gradient computation, while Continuous-DTW (CDTW) introduces a continuous formulation through parametrizable warping functions. Yet, computational costs remain high for both methods and impractical for large datasets in modern machine learning pipelines. This paper revisits CDTW in several ways. After establishing its differentiability under mild conditions, we introduce FastCDTW, which is an efficient approximate solver with two different computational strategies: an exact closed-form scheme for piecewise-linear warping functions, and an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for smooth ones, such as implicit neural networks. Both strategies provide gradients with respect to the warping function and the input time series, and the resulting algorithm is GPU-friendly. We demonstrate its benefits through its integration into more complex learning problems, including time series averaging, classification and deep domain adaptation.

entry.title: Fast Rates for Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization

link.title: Fast Rates for Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization

entry.content:
Weighted empirical risk minimization is a common approach to prediction under distribution drift. This article studies its out-of-sample prediction error under nonstationarity. We provide a general decomposition of the excess risk into a learning term and an error term associated with distribution drift, and prove oracle inequalities for the learning error under mixing conditions. The learning bound holds uniformly over arbitrary weight classes and accounts for the effective sample size induced by the weight vector, the complexity of the weight and hypothesis classes, and potential data dependence. We also analyze the drift error in the square loss setting and provide explicit bounds for structural-break and smoothly drifting processes. We then combine the learning and drift analysis in (auto-) regression problems with linear models, basis approximations, and neural networks. In all cases, the optimal weights are characterized by a bias–variance trade-off between learning and drift, while minimax-optimal rates (up to logarithmic factors) are recovered when specialized to unweighted and stationary settings.

entry.title: Federated Learning of Nonlinear Temporal Dynamics with Graph Attention-based Cross-Client Interpretability

link.title: Federated Learning of Nonlinear Temporal Dynamics with Graph Attention-based Cross-Client Interpretability

entry.content:
Networks of modern industrial systems are increasingly monitored by distributed sensors, where each system comprises multiple subsystems that generate high-dimensional time-series. These subsystems are often interdependent, making it important to understand how temporal patterns observed at one subsystem relate to those observed across others. This problem is particularly challenging in decentralized settings where raw measurements cannot be shared, and client observations are heterogeneous. Moreover, in practice, each subsystem (client) operates a fixed, proprietary model that cannot be modified or retrained, limiting the applicability of existing approaches. Separately, nonlinear dynamics make cross-client temporal interdependencies difficult to characterize, as they are embedded implicitly within nonlinear state-transition functions. This paper presents a vertical federated learning framework for learning one-step-ahead cross-client temporal interdependencies under these constraints. Each client maps high-dimensional local observations to low-dimensional latent states using a nonlinear state-space model, while a Graph Attention Network (GAT)-based central server learns a state-transition model over the communicated states. Given a candidate graph skeleton, the server learns state-dependent attention coefficients that capture cross-client interactions. We analytically relate the GAT attention coefficients to the Jacobian of the learned state-transition model, yielding a first-order characterization of cross-client interdependencies. We further establish bounded closeness of the learned dynamics and Jacobians to a corresponding centralized oracle. Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical results on controlled systems with known graph skeletons. Experiments on real-world datasets with unknown graph skeletons demonstrate superior federated root cause analysis over baselines.

entry.title: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Fully Discrete Conditional Diffusion Models

link.title: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Fully Discrete Conditional Diffusion Models

entry.content:
We establish finite-sample guarantees for conditional diffusion models learned from data and implemented with finitely many denoising steps. Our approach aligns the score-training objective with the sampling grid, allowing statistical estimation and numerical discretization errors to be analyzed together. Under a smooth conditional density model, we derive high-probability bounds on the generated distribution’s error and quantify the required number of score evaluations. For every smoothness index $\beta>0$, a suitable grid yields averaged conditional Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence $\widetilde O_p(n^{-2\beta/(d_x+d_y+2\beta)})$ relative to the original target with or without early stopping. Both the full and early-stopped samplers attain average target total-variation (TV) error $\widetilde O_p(n^{-\beta/(d_x+d_y+2\beta)})$. Here $n$ is the sample size, $d_x,d_y$ are the data and conditioning dimensions, and errors are averaged over the conditioning variable. The total-variation bound matches the rate established in existing conditional distribution-estimation theory, up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: Forecasting Corpus-Sampling Disagreement in Masked Text Reconstruction

link.title: Forecasting Corpus-Sampling Disagreement in Masked Text Reconstruction

entry.content:
If a second text corpus were collected from the same population, how much would a predictor’s outputs change? We study this question for masked-text reconstruction using a smoothed predictor built from nearby token-pair counts and evaluated over the full 50,257-token GPT-2 vocabulary. Treating each source document as one observation, we derive a first-order formula for the expected disagreement between predictors fitted to two independent corpora. The formula accounts for variable document length, random context counts, and correlations across token offsets, and it can be evaluated from a separate reference corpus without access to either target corpus. On TinyStories, WikiText-103, and CNN/DailyMail, growing each corpus from 512 to 2,048 chunks of 64 tokens lowers disagreement by only 5–40\%, far short of the 75\% implied by $1/n$ scaling. The forecast tracks this slow decline, which we trace to smoothing of rarely seen contexts. Forecast accuracy depends less on how these correlations are modeled than on the size of the reference corpus: small references systematically underpredict disagreement. A source-split jackknife that uses only reference data reduces this calibration error by 57–59\%. After this correction, a simpler smoothed-multinomial approximation is most accurate when the reference corpus is smaller than the target corpus, and a nonlinear source bootstrap is most accurate when it is larger. Finally, small masked diffusion language models trained on the same corpora show that the count-based forecasts partly identify which inputs are most sensitive to the corpus, but miss the neural models’ much faster decline in disagreement.

entry.title: From Imbalance to Evidence: Deep Nonparametric Testing for Complex Data under Severe Sample Imbalance

link.title: From Imbalance to Evidence: Deep Nonparametric Testing for Complex Data under Severe Sample Imbalance

entry.content:
Comparing distributions under severe sample imbalance requires effectively using abundant majority observations while retaining sensitivity to differences involving the smaller sample. This challenge is particularly relevant for complex, non-Euclidean data, such as graphs, whose structural characteristics call for flexible testing procedures. Classifier two-sample tests (C2STs) provide such flexibility, but existing procedures are primarily designed for balanced or comparably sized samples. In this paper, we study C2STs in a highly imbalanced regime, and show that severe sample imbalance may substantially degrade testing performance. Different from conventional imbalanced learning approaches that treat sample imbalance merely as a nuisance for classifier training, we turn it into a source of repeated testing evidence. Building on this insight, we propose an Enhanced Imbalance-Aware Deep Classifier Two-Sample Test (EIAD-C2ST), a classifier-agnostic framework designed for sample imbalance that accommodates diverse data modalities by tailoring classifiers to data structure. For computationally expensive deep classifiers, we further develop a scalable representation-amortized implementation strategy. Theoretically, we establish rigorous guarantees on asymptotic size and characterize conditions for power consistency, allowing the imbalance ratio to diverge. We demonstrate the empirical gains using simulations and an application to blockchain forensics. The results reveal that the majority-sample surplus, when properly leveraged, can be organized into useful statistical evidence, rather than an obstacle, for distributional comparisons with complex data.

entry.title: From Pixels to Privacy-Sensitive Features: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Reconstruction Bounds

link.title: From Pixels to Privacy-Sensitive Features: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Reconstruction Bounds

entry.content:
What can an adversary recover from a model trained with DP-SGD? Its $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ guarantee does not answer this question directly. We derive a distortion bound that can be computed before training and applies even to an adversary who observes the parameter trajectory during training, knows every other training record and the population distribution from which the training records are drawn. The analyst may choose the representation in which error is measured, allowing the bound to target the aspects of reconstruction that are privacy-sensitive in a given application. Our information-theoretic framework separates two contributions: the information about a record revealed by training, measured through conditional mutual information, and the uncertainty already present in the data distribution, measured through source entropy. Rate-distortion theory combines them into a lower bound on the expected error of every reconstruction attack. For DP-SGD, the leakage bound depends only on the sampling rates and noise multipliers, while the source entropy is lower-bounded from a sample with finite-sample confidence. An orthogonal block construction keeps the resulting bound informative for high-dimensional images. We instantiate the framework in pixel space and in LPIPS feature space, obtaining, to our knowledge, the first lower bound on reconstruction distortion measured directly by LPIPS. On a range of image datasets the bounds establish non-trivial unavoidable expected reconstruction error within heuristically recommended privacy-budget ranges and beyond. Experiments compare the bounds with strong reconstruction attacks and identify the principal sources of the remaining slack.

link.title: Gaussian BROJA Partial Information Decomposition in Closed Form

entry.content:
The BROJA partial information decomposition provides an operationally motivated way to separate the information that two sources carry about a target into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. For continuous and high-dimensional variables, however, computing the BROJA decomposition requires solving a difficult optimization problem. Previous work showed that, when each source-target pair is jointly Gaussian, the problem can be reduced to finite-dimensional numerical optimization. Here, we derive a closed-form solution to this optimization problem, enabling direct computation of the BROJA decomposition in the general multivariate Gaussian setting. The resulting closed-form expression enables speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high-dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID. Code is available at https://github.com/brainsandmachines/Eigen_PID.

entry.title: Generalized Determinantal Point Processes for Attraction and Repulsion with Distinct Interaction Kernels

link.title: Generalized Determinantal Point Processes for Attraction and Repulsion with Distinct Interaction Kernels

entry.content:
Determinantal point processes (DPPs) model subset selection probability with repulsion, but many applications also exhibit attraction arising from pairwise relations or shared latent structures. Nonsymmetric DPPs (NDPPs) capture both effects, but their kernels are difficult to interpret and specify. We propose the determinant-ratio point process (DRPP), which models repulsion and attraction via a ratio of the determinants of two symmetric positive-definite kernels. This formulation preserves the feature-based interpretation of standard DPPs while allowing the two effects to be specified separately. Furthermore, we introduce an auxiliary-variable representation that enables efficient MCMC sampling and yields tractable expectation formulas for key statistics including the normalizing constant, which together facilitate maximum-likelihood learning. We theoretically characterize the interaction structures well suited to DRPPs: for clustered attraction with $C$ latent groups, DRPPs exactly realize the target pairwise interactions with an attraction rank $C$, whereas NDPPs can require a rank that grows with the number of items given the same repulsion component. Conversely, nontransitive pair-specific attraction may require compensation through the DRPP repulsion kernel. Experiments support these predictions, showing that DRPPs fit transitive attraction with substantially fewer parameters than NDPPs.

entry.title: Hitting-Time Bounds for Asynchronous Q-Learning

link.title: Hitting-Time Bounds for Asynchronous Q-Learning

entry.content:
We study the last iterate of standard asynchronous Q-learning from a single trajectory of a finite Markov decision process. The trajectory follows a fixed behavior policy whose state–action chain is irreducible and may be periodic. For discount factor $\gamma$, write $H=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and let $\mu_{\min}$ be the minimum stationary state–action probability and $\mathfrak h_\star$ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse state–action chain. We prove that zero-initialized Q-learning with a constant step size achieves sup-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ with high probability using $\widetilde{O}(H^4/(\mu_{\min}\varepsilon^2)+\mathfrak h_\star)$ transitions, for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The statistical term retains the quartic effective-horizon dependence of standard Q-learning, while initialization cost is additive in $\mathfrak h_\star$. For aperiodic behavior chains, a comparison with mixing time yields a transient term $\widetilde{O}(t_{\mathrm{mix}}/\mu_{\min})$. An empirical state–action count rule selects a constant step size for a subsequent training run and attains the same rate without prior knowledge of model parameters, target accuracy, or confidence level. The output is the last training iterate, with both stages included in the sample count. The proof uses two deterministic Bellman envelopes to separate statistical error from fixed-policy initialization error and adapts reverse-time hitting-cost compensation from TD learning to state–action propagation. An exploration lower bound holds for arbitrary predictable step sizes. Together with the existing statistical lower bound and its extension to pilot-selected constant steps, it yields matching mean-square rates up to logarithmic factors on the stated large-sample parameter classes.

entry.title: How Many Significant LISA?: A multiple testing correction

link.title: How Many Significant LISA?: A multiple testing correction

entry.content:
In spatial data analysis, global measures of spatial correlation provide useful insights into the general spatial patterns, but fail to capture local variations. Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) address this limitation by identifying local clusters and spatial outliers, offering valuable applications in many fields of research such as public health, urban planning and environmental monitoring, to name only a few. However, the application of LISA tools in hypothesis testing is undermined by the presence of the multiple testing problem which dramatically increases the risk of committing Type I errors especially when dealing with very large datasets. Standard corrections procedure (like, e. g., Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures) fail to consider the spatial dependence among the various LISA tests and, furthermore, they are overly conservative. This paper proposes an adjustment that, by incorporating the notion of the “effective sample size”, improves statistical inference balancing false discovery rate control and statistical power.

entry.summary: In spatial data analysis, global measures of spatial correlation provide useful insights into the general spatial patterns, but fail to capture local variations. Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) address this limitation by identifying local clusters and spatial outliers, offering valuable applications in many fields of research such as public health, urban planning and environmental monitoring, to name only a few. However, the application of LISA tools in hypothesis testing is undermined by the presence of the multiple testing problem which dramatically increases the risk of committing Type I errors especially when dealing with very large datasets. Standard corrections procedure (like, e. g., Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures) fail to consider the spatial dependence among the various LISA tests and, furthermore, they are overly conservative. This paper proposes an adjustment that, by incorporating the notion of the “effective sample size”, improves statistical inference balancing false discovery rate control and statistical power.

entry.title: How Well Do Prior-Data Fitted Networks Amortize Bayesian Inference?

link.title: How Well Do Prior-Data Fitted Networks Amortize Bayesian Inference?

entry.content:
Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution (PPD) of a synthetic prior, yet results about the approximation quality are surprisingly thin. Taking an empirical risk minimization perspective, we decompose the deployment error of PFNs into prior, context, and amortization error, and measure the latter against a reference PPD under a realistic prior. Results show that PFNs generally recover the targeted PPD very well. Nevertheless, we find that parts of the residual amortization error persist, especially in \textit{rare} settings under the prior pretraining distribution, even when scaling the model size, which manifests in disagreement between independently pretrained PFNs and leaves uncertainty about the predictor at inference time. As a remedy, we study multiple types of Bayesian model averages and find that these can consistently reduce this uncertainty and improve predictions up to full-size TabICLv2 models.

entry.title: Infinitesimal Operator World Models: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Offline Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Infinitesimal Operator World Models: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Offline Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
Continuous-time stochastic processes underlie many natural and engineered systems. In healthcare, autonomous driving, and industrial control, direct interaction with the environment is often unsafe or impractical, motivating offline reinforcement learning from historical data. However, there is limited statistical understanding of the approximation errors inherent in learning policies from offline datasets. We address this by linking reinforcement learning to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation and proposing an operator-theoretic algorithm based on a simple dynamic programming recursion. Specifically, we represent our world model in terms of the infinitesimal generator of controlled diffusion processes learned in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By integrating statistical learning methods and operator theory, we establish global convergence of the value function under sufficiently small generator-approximation error and derive explicit finite-sample guarantees with bounds tied directly to system properties such as smoothness and stability. Our theoretical and proof-of-concept results indicate that operator-based approaches may hold promise for solving offline reinforcement learning using continuous-time optimal control.

entry.title: Interval-valued circular time series: A toroidal score-driven approach with an application to wind direction

link.title: Interval-valued circular time series: A toroidal score-driven approach with an application to wind direction

entry.content:
Circular data recorded over time, such as wind direction, are increasingly observed in intervals rather than as single point-valued observations, yet no existing framework accommodates data that are simultaneously circular, interval-valued, and temporally dependent. Time series models for point-valued circular data, including recently proposed score-driven approaches, assume that each observation is a single angle. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a dynamic conditional score framework for interval-valued circular time series. The lower and upper boundary sequences of the observed intervals are treated as circular time series governed by score-driven dynamics, which preserves the periodicity of the circular domain and the dependency of boundaries, in which the boundaries are coupled through a toroidal distribution and a jointly derived score. Maximum likelihood estimation is discussed, and their finite-sample performance is evaluated through simulation. An application to interval-valued wind direction data illustrates the practical value of retaining the interval structure within a fully rotationally invariant circular framework.

entry.title: Is Inference Conditional on Not Rejecting a Pre-test Less Reliable than Unconditional Inference?

link.title: Is Inference Conditional on Not Rejecting a Pre-test Less Reliable than Unconditional Inference?

entry.content:
Researchers often report an estimate and confidence interval only if a specification test does not reject - for example, only if a pre-trend test supports a difference-in-differences design. Does this make the reported confidence interval less reliable? We show that when the identifying assumptions hold, the answer is no: conditional on passing the pre-test, the confidence interval may over-cover but cannot under-cover. When the assumptions fail, pre-testing can reduce coverage, but under an additional condition it still improves coverage relative to not pre-testing. A calibration to 12 differences-in-differences examples suggests modest effects of pre-testing on coverage.

entry.title: Kernel-based External Validity of Experimental Studies

link.title: Kernel-based External Validity of Experimental Studies

entry.content:
The external validity of a study is the extent to which its findings generalize to unseen experimental conditions, such as datasets. We formalize the results of a study together with its research question, and define external validity as the probability that two independent and same-sized replications of the study produce results whose maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is below a given tolerance. This approach, centered on the choice of a space of results and of an appropriate reproducing kernel for the MMD, is flexible enough to be deployed on multiple different types of results and research questions. Additionally, we establish an asymptotic power-law relation between the size of a study and the quantiles of the MMD, which we use to estimate the desired size of an externally valid study from a small-scale preliminary study. We deploy our framework to rankings with ties and discuss kernels suited to different research questions. Experiments on existing case studies and on a simulated newly designed study illustrate the applicability of the framework. We release our code as part of the genexpy Python module.

entry.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability

link.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability

entry.content:
Gradient-based attribution provides input-specific information about model parameters, but computing it via backpropagation for many samples is expensive, while static importance scores discard input dependence. We derive KPSA (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel. It measures normalized parameter-group sensitivity, embeds those sources in an explicit query space, and uses a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs. We derive bounds that separate finite-source from irreducible representation error and give margin-based top-$k$ recovery. This paper studies two interpretability applications. Firstly, KPSA identifies parameter groups with high susceptibility to perturbations across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups. Across a fivefold range of parameter budgets ($0.02$-$0.1\%$), its selected groups attain $39$-$85\%$ of the perturbation susceptibility of a first-order backpropagation oracle. In vision and forecasting, these parameter groups form sparse sensitivity circuits that extend across depth and vary systematically with the input. Secondly, we use KPSA on an activation-attribution problem for MLP features in transformers. It retains $81\%$ of the gap between a backpropagation oracle and a constant-sensitivity baseline on vision while increasing batched query-time throughput from 551 to 2,041 images/s and reducing peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44GB. On the protein-modeling task, it recovers $68\%$ of this gap. An ablation of KPSA’s kernel aggregation shows that nearest-neighbor retrieval in KPSA space can remain competitive. The empirics show that compact kernel atlases can store useful input-dependent parameter sensitivity while amortizing repeated gradient attribution, a step toward scalable conditional interpretability. Code can be found at https://github.com/Axym-Labs/kpsa .

entry.title: Latent-Class Poisson-Lognormal Mixed Models for Clustering Multivariate Longitudinal Count Data

link.title: Latent-Class Poisson-Lognormal Mixed Models for Clustering Multivariate Longitudinal Count Data

entry.content:
Multivariate longitudinal count data arise in biological studies, where responses may be over-dispersed, correlated within subjects and over time, measured at irregular times, and exhibit unobserved subgroup structure. Our goal was to develop a model that can accommodate over-dispersion, longitudinal dependence, cross-outcome dependence, covariate effects, irregular observation times, and covariate-dependent latent-class membership. We propose a latent-class Poisson-lognormal mixed model for clustering heterogeneous multivariate count trajectories. Estimation is performed using a variational EM algorithm designed for scalable inference. Simulation studies show accurate parameter estimation, strong latent-class recovery, and reliable selection of the number of classes, as compared to state-of-the-art approaches. We also applied the proposed approach to longitudinal neutrophil RNA-seq data from hospitalized COVID-19 patients as an illustration. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for clustering complex longitudinal biological count data. Implementation code is available at https://github.com/PengqiLiu-Mc/latent-class-mpln-mixed-models.

entry.title: Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention

link.title: Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention

entry.content:
Social influence, the tendency of our social environment to sway our beliefs and behaviors, is often cited as a driver of population-level trends in opinions or beliefs. Many quantitative theories of social influence assume that an agent interacts with its entire social environment. This assumption is often unrealistic. For example, users of online platforms typically see posts from only a small subset of the accounts they follow at any given time. We introduce a simple probabilistic agent-based model of social influence that explicitly models unobserved attention mechanisms. The first of these latent mechanisms is selection: each agent interacts with only one other agent at a time from its social environment. The second is retention: the agent chooses whether or not to ignore the opinion of the other. Our model admits an efficient maximum-likelihood algorithm which allows us to fit it to opinion traces even when these mechanisms are unobserved. On synthetic data, omitting either latent mechanism reduces the overall strength of social influence governed by the inferred interaction kernel, which hides the evidence for the underlying nonlinearity of the social influence. We study a selection of previously analyzed empirical datasets and curate several new ones. We show that models that include the latent mechanisms are often more predictive on these datasets; indeed, they typically improve prediction far more than the choice of interaction kernel does. Modeling latent attention increases held-out predictive likelihood on 14 of these 15 datasets. Each mechanism changes the size of the inferred kernel in a predictable direction, while its effect on the kernel’s shape depends on the data.

entry.title: Learning by Compression: Risk Estimates Attain the Law-of-Large-Numbers Rate

link.title: Learning by Compression: Risk Estimates Attain the Law-of-Large-Numbers Rate

entry.content:
Compression schemes provide a general framework for deriving data-dependent risk bounds for learning algorithms. For learning rules based on preferent compression, existing results upper-bound the risk in terms of a sample-dependent complexity $\boldsymbol{k}$, defined as the cardinality of the compression augmented by the training examples on which the reconstructed hypothesis is inappropriate. These results, however, yield a margin of order $O(\sqrt{\ln N/N})$ above $\boldsymbol{k}/N$. In this paper, we establish that the logarithmic factor is not intrinsic. We prove that, for every fixed confidence level $1-\delta$, the risk is bounded with probability at least $1-\delta$ by \(\frac{\boldsymbol{k}}{N} + O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right),\) uniformly over all possible values of $\boldsymbol{k}$. Thus, risk estimates for learning algorithms based on preferent compression attain the same law-of-large-numbers rate as the empirical estimate of the probability of a fixed event. We also show that the leading term $\boldsymbol{k}/N$ is necessary and investigate its relation to the empirical risk. In particular, we identify regimes in which the empirical risk retains the $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ convergence rate, as well as regimes in which it converges more slowly or ceases to be consistent, while the complexity-based estimator preserves the $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ rate.

entry.title: Linearized Wasserstein dimensionality reduction with approximation guarantees

link.title: Linearized Wasserstein dimensionality reduction with approximation guarantees

entry.content:
We introduce LOT Wassmap, a computationally feasible algorithm to uncover low-dimensional structures in the Wasserstein space. The algorithm is motivated by the observation that many datasets are naturally interpreted as probability measures rather than points in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and that finding low-dimensional descriptions of such datasets requires manifold learning algorithms in the Wasserstein space. Most available algorithms are based on computing the pairwise Wasserstein distance matrix, which can be computationally challenging for large datasets in high dimensions. Our algorithm leverages approximation schemes such as Sinkhorn distances and linearized optimal transport to speed-up computations, and in particular, avoids computing a pairwise distance matrix. We provide guarantees on the embedding quality under such approximations, including when explicit descriptions of the probability measures are not available and one must deal with finite samples instead. Experiments demonstrate that LOT Wassmap attains correct embeddings and that the quality improves with increased sample size. We also show how LOT Wassmap significantly reduces the computational cost when compared to algorithms that depend on pairwise distance computations.

entry.title: Locally Private Parametric Methods for Change-Point Detection

link.title: Locally Private Parametric Methods for Change-Point Detection

entry.content:
We study parametric change-point detection under local differential privacy, focusing on the offline localization of a single change point in a sequence of independent observations.~In the non-private setting, we derive improved finite-sample accuracy guarantees for a generalized likelihood-ratio estimator using martingale methods.~We establish finite-sample minimax lower bounds in both the non-private and locally private settings, showing that localization accuracy is fundamentally limited by the Chernoff information between the pre- and post-change distributions.~Guided by this, we design locally private CPD algorithms based on aggregated randomized response and binary mechanisms, which maximize the Chernoff information between the induced output distributions in low- and high-privacy regimes, respectively, and derive their finite-sample guarantees. Together, our upper and lower bounds quantify the statistical cost of privacy in change-point localization.~As part of our analysis, we also show that strong data processing inequality coefficients of R'enyi divergence and Jeffreys–R'enyi divergence of order infinity can be computed by restricting to pairs of input distributions with a common support of at most two symbols.~We corroborate our results through empirical evaluation on synthetic data.

entry.title: Markov Chain Convergence in Kernel-Induced Geometry

link.title: Markov Chain Convergence in Kernel-Induced Geometry

entry.content:
We study the convergence of Markov chains in the geometry induced by Hilbertian embeddings associated with positive definite kernels, also called Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Under a contraction assumption in the kernel-induced geometry, and a standard spectral gap assumption, we establish non-asymptotic, high-probability bounds for the convergence of the empirical occupation measure to the invariant measure. The obtained bounds separate the roles of the two conditions: the spectral gap determines the effective sample size in the leading term, while the kernel contraction enters only through a linear correction. As an application, we study one-step prediction of dynamical systems from a single trajectory, deriving fast learning rates for a nonlinear least-squares estimator. The rates highlight the interplay between mixing properties in the kernel-induced geometry and the classical source and capacity conditions used in the analysis of least-squares.

entry.title: Minimax Rates for Estimating Powered Sliced Wasserstein Functionals

link.title: Minimax Rates for Estimating Powered Sliced Wasserstein Functionals

entry.content:
We study the two-sample estimation of the powered Sliced Wasserstein functional under projected $r$-th moment assumptions. Let $N=n\wedge m$, where $n$ and $m$ are two sample sizes. We establish the minimax rates in the noncritical regimes. When $p<2p$, the minimax risk is of order $N^{-(r-p)/r}$, while for $r>2p$ it is of order $N^{-1/2}$. In both cases, the natural plug-in estimator is minimax rate-optimal. At the endpoint $r=p$, the minimax risk is bounded away from zero, so uniformly consistent estimation is impossible. At the critical order $r=2p$, we obtain the exact worst-case rate of the plug-in estimator and a lower bound for the minimax risk, leaving a logarithmic gap between the lower and upper bounds. The exact minimax rate in this critical case remains open.
