entry.title: Minimax Rates for Learning Smooth Populations of Parameters

link.title: Minimax Rates for Learning Smooth Populations of Parameters

entry.content:
We study pointwise estimation of a smooth binomial mixing density and characterize its minimax rates. Assuming that the mixing density is $s$-H"older smooth, we first consider the homogeneous setting with a common number of binomial trials $t$. We derive matching lower and upper bounds that reveal three regimes depending on the relative sizes of the sample size $n$ and the number of trials $t$. When $t$ is small, the finite number of trials creates an identification barrier that persists regardless of sample size; at intermediate $t$, more data reduce sampling uncertainty, while the number of trials limits how finely the mixing density can be recovered; and when $t$ is sufficiently large, the usual nonparametric density estimation rate is recovered. Our lower bounds exploit the polynomial structure of the binomial mixture model, while attainability is achieved by a suitably regularized orthogonal series estimator. We then extend the analysis to heterogeneous trial parameters, where the minimax rate depends on the full trial profile through the effective sample size available at each polynomial degree. These results characterize the fundamental statistical limits of learning smooth populations of binomial probabilities under both homogeneous and heterogeneous trials.

link.title: Model-free Bayesian Clustering and Multimodal Posterior Summarisation

entry.content:
We develop a model-free, noise-aware Bayesian clustering framework that constructs a martingale posterior over clusterings from a predictive Bayesian perspective. This avoids explicit likelihood-prior model specification, expensive MCMC sampling, and mode-seeking variational approximations, while accommodating irregular cluster shapes and enabling parallel generation of posterior draws. To interpret the posterior over high-dimensional, noise-aware clusterings, we introduce a Wasserstein-type summarization method. Using a novel noise-aware loss, this approach compresses the large collection of posterior draws into a small set of weighted representatives, capturing distinct cluster structures and noise assignments. Further, we marginalise the uncertainty in the density level, avoiding reliance on a specific choice. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed loss and guarantees for the level-marginal posterior approximation. Results demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in capturing clustering and noise uncertainty.

entry.title: Near-Minimax-Optimal Rates for Asynchronous TD Learning with Markovian Data

link.title: Near-Minimax-Optimal Rates for Asynchronous TD Learning with Markovian Data

entry.content:
We study the last iterate of standard importance-weighted temporal-difference (TD) learning from a single trajectory of a finite Markov decision process. The trajectory follows a behavior policy $b$ with an irreducible, possibly periodic state chain; a target policy $\pi$ covered by $b$ is evaluated with action importance ratios bounded by $\varrho$. Write $H=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, with $\mu_{\min}$ the minimum stationary probability and $\mathfrak h_\star$ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse behavior state chain. We prove that the last iterate achieves sup-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ with high probability after $\widetilde O(\varrho H^3/(\mu_{\min}\varepsilon^2)+\mathfrak h_\star)$ transitions for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The statistical term retains the cubic effective-horizon dependence of synchronous TD, while the initialization cost is additive in $\mathfrak h_\star$. Setting $b=\pi$ and $\varrho=1$ recovers the on-policy rate. For aperiodic behavior chains, $\mathfrak h_\star=\widetilde O(t_{\rm mix}/\mu_{\min})$ recovers a mixing-time bound. The proof combines an anchored local Poisson equation in reverse time to control fluctuations without a mixing-time factor, a compensation argument for successive hitting costs, and an expected cumulative propagation mass bound for decreasing step sizes. Given the policy ratios and their bound, an empirical state-count rule attains the same rate without prior knowledge of model parameters. The framework covers nonnegative affine importance-weighted prediction updates, including successor features, transition-dependent discounting, and coupled finite-mode predictions. A perturbation estimate yields a time-uniform guarantee for online return-variance estimation. A three-state, two-action construction gives matching minimax lower bounds for both terms up to logarithmic factors on the considered parameter classes.

entry.title: Neural Estimation of Summary Statistics for Simulation-Based Inference with Non-Asymptotic Guarantees

link.title: Neural Estimation of Summary Statistics for Simulation-Based Inference with Non-Asymptotic Guarantees

entry.content:
Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables Bayesian inference when a simulator is available but the likelihood is intractable. Modern SBI methods train neural networks on simulated data to obtain an amortized approximation of the posterior, making inference for new observations fast. A central challenge in SBI is to extract informative, low-dimensional summary statistics; without them, performance can degrade rapidly as the observation dimension grows. We therefore highlight summary learning as a critical component of SBI and propose a general framework that jointly learns a neural-network-parameterized summary and an amortized posterior estimator. We further introduce a local refinement strategy that adapts the amortized estimator to a specific observation, thereby reducing the amortization gap. Both amortized training and local refinement accommodate implicit posterior estimators without tractable densities. On the theoretical side, we analyze the finite-sample behavior of the joint learning procedure through the lens of nonparametric conditional distribution estimation, and show on representative examples how low-dimensional summaries can mitigate the classical curse of dimensionality. Empirically, our results support this motivation and demonstrate favorable performance relative to existing methods.

entry.title: Neural posterior inference with state-space models for calibrating ice sheet simulators

link.title: Neural posterior inference with state-space models for calibrating ice sheet simulators

entry.content:
Ice sheet models are routinely used to quantify and project an ice sheet’s contribution to sea level rise. In order for an ice sheet model to generate realistic projections, its parameters must first be calibrated using observational data; this is challenging due to the nonlinearity of the model equations, the high dimensionality of the underlying parameters, and limited data availability for validation. This study leverages the emerging field of neural posterior approximation for efficiently calibrating ice sheet model parameters and boundary conditions. We make use of a one-dimensional (flowline) Shallow-Shelf Approximation model in a state-space framework. A neural network is trained to infer the underlying parameters, namely the bedrock elevation and basal friction coefficient along the flowline, based on observations of ice velocity and ice surface elevation. Samples from the approximate posterior distribution of the parameters are then used within an ensemble Kalman filter to infer latent model states, namely the ice thickness along the flowline. We show through a simulation study that our approach yields more accurate estimates of the parameters and states than a state-augmented ensemble Kalman filter, which is the current state-of-the-art. We apply our approach to infer the bed elevation and basal friction along a flowline in Thwaites Glacier, Antarctica.

entry.title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels

link.title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels

entry.content:
Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query-key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization (OAL), a dimension-aware method for constructing quadratic attention approximations. Starting from a second-order Taylor approximation, we introduce a Hadamard-product formulation that makes individual query-key contributions explicit. This formulation relaxes globally shared coefficients to support dimension-specific linear terms and cross-dimensional quadratic interactions while preserving separable evaluation. To retain this flexibility with fewer parameters, OAL groups dimensions with similar contribution scales to share coefficients, while allowing distinct treatment of the few outliers. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and admits linear-time evaluation with respect to sequence length for fixed head dimensions. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% compared with DiJiang. Replacing middle-layer attention modules and jointly fine-tuning the kernel coefficients with LoRA further lowers WikiText-103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 compared with a learned global quadratic, while improving accuracy on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E. These results demonstrate the value of outlier-aware dimension grouping for both attention approximation and pretrained-model conversion. The code is available at https://github.com/wuqianyue09/OAL

entry.title: Occam’s Razor is Only as Sharp as Your ELBO

link.title: Occam’s Razor is Only as Sharp as Your ELBO

entry.content:
The marginal likelihood, also known as the evidence, is regarded as a mathematical embodiment of Occam’s razor, enabling hyperparameter selection that avoids overfitting. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) objective from variational inference has also been used for similar purposes. In this paper, we define a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for Bayesian linear regression in terms of key hyperparameters controlling signal and noise variance. We then study how ELBO-based hyperparameter learning can under or overestimate SNR depending on the assumed covariance matrix structure in a Gaussian approximate posterior. We prove that assuming a diagonal or low-rank plus diagonal covariance matrix underestimates the SNR, while a low-rank covariance matrix overestimates the SNR. Underestimating the SNR leads to higher than optimal mean squared error on the training set (underfitting), while overestimating SNR leads to lower error (overfitting). Bayesian practitioners hoping to scale to large models should be cautious about how covariance assumptions needed for tractability may impact model selection.

entry.title: One Thing Leads to Another: The Essentials of Time Series Causal Discovery

link.title: One Thing Leads to Another: The Essentials of Time Series Causal Discovery

entry.content:
Time series causal discovery — the process of detecting causation between time series — has its roots in signal processing research from over a half century ago. It has since received active and widespread interest, evolving into different forms across domains such as statistics, dynamical systems and machine learning. Entering this fragmented and constantly evolving research landscape can be daunting. This tutorial provides a unified overview of time series causal discovery across research communities. We introduce the key principles invoked by modern discovery methods, and we discuss their limitations and assumptions. We also discuss how discovery methods are evaluated, benchmarked and fine-tuned. We further discuss how causal discovery for time series is becoming crucial for downstream tasks in agriculture and Earth science, in healthcare, and in artificial intelligence systems. We believe that this tutorial will serve as a valuable resource in navigating the deluge of recent causality research, as well as an invitation to signal processing audiences to contribute to causal problems. To further help readers, we host a companion repository to link to useful code packages and resources at https://github.com/CHAI-UK/Awesome-Time-Series-Causal-Discovery.

entry.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons—a statistical look at the METR plot

link.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons—a statistical look at the METR plot

entry.content:
METR’s 50\% time horizon measures the human completion time of software tasks that an AI solves with 50\% probability, allowing AI capabilities to be expressed in interpretable units. On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, we recompute the time horizons using splines and item-response theory to relax the assumption that the AI difficulty of a task depends linearly on the log of human time. Our fitted spline can be interpreted as a function that \emph{converts} human time to AI difficulty; it is nearly flat in a region from 2–30 min but close to linear elsewhere. Hence, a time-horizon jump from 3 min to 30 min is much easier than one from 30 min to 5 hours despite the same multiplier of $10 \times$. Overall, we contribute time-horizon point estimates that perform better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, as well as diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons’ construct validity. We suggest that time horizons be interpreted together with the diagnostic plots, especially as new time-horizon-based benchmarks are proposed or existing ones grow to include longer tasks.

entry.title: Optimizable Model Averaging for Ensembling Heterogeneous Model Outputs

link.title: Optimizable Model Averaging for Ensembling Heterogeneous Model Outputs

entry.content:
Foundation model ensembles can improve accuracy and robustness, but full fine-tuning and parameter-space merging are often expensive or impossible when candidate models have different architectures. We propose Optimizable Model Averaging (OMA), a black-box approach that learns nonnegative model-combination weights, one scalar coefficient per model, to average the candidate models’ predictive probabilities, leaving all model parameters frozen, by minimizing regularized predictive entropy. A central challenge is that minimizing predictive entropy can favour confidently incorrect models: increased confidence need not imply improved accuracy or calibration. We therefore examine regularization as a mechanism for controlling adaptation and empirically evaluate its effect on calibration, observing lower expected calibration error in selected configurations, alongside better performance-calibration trade-offs than model output averaging. As foundation models continue to advance, these approaches will enable the incorporation of future, potentially much better models to improve performance on challenging text and image classification tasks.

entry.title: Particle-based Generalised Stochastic Optimisation

link.title: Particle-based Generalised Stochastic Optimisation

entry.content:
We develop a class of general diffusion-based stochastic particle optimisation methods for loss functions with intractable gradients. Specifically, we consider problems in which the loss gradient is an integral with respect to a parameter-dependent distribution, a structure that includes training generative models, fine-tuning, and learning latent-variable models. We introduce mean-field dynamics and its interacting-particle approximations, which contain several existing algorithms as special cases and provide a route to constructing new methods. Under well-posedness and joint contractivity assumptions, we prove exponential convergence and show that the continuous-time particle system admits a non-asymptotic error bound. We illustrate our framework by developing higher-order Langevin and momentum optimisers and evaluating them on maximum marginal-likelihood estimation and energy-based-model training.

entry.title: Predictive-Context LOO: Bayesian Model Comparison with Pretrained Predictive Learners

link.title: Predictive-Context LOO: Bayesian Model Comparison with Pretrained Predictive Learners

entry.content:
Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation, a standard tool for Bayesian model assessment, evaluates each observation using a LOO predictive distribution derived from the model itself. In this work, we introduce an alternative construction in which posterior predictive simulation connects the Bayesian model to an external pretrained predictive learner. Our method, Predictive-Context LOO (PC-LOO), fits a Bayesian model once, generates posterior-predictive synthetic data, and uses them as context for the learner to approximate each LOO predictive density. Under an oracle construction, averaging contexts generated from the LOO posterior recovers the exact LOO predictive density. Practical PC-LOO replaces the oracle predictor by the pretrained learner and the LOO posterior by the full posterior. We quantify these errors through learner compatibility $C_i$ and deletion influence $V_i$, obtaining $H^2 (p^{LOO}{i} , q^{PC}{i}) \leq C_{i} + V_{i}$. The identity also holds for any fixed subset of $M$ context points, allowing $M \ll n - 1$ as the learner’s context budget, and scalability to large datasets. Experiments with TabICL support this decomposition, deletion influence decays approximately as $n^{-1}$, while learner compatibility can remain limiting at large $n$. PC-LOO remains accurate with reduced context sizes, while model comparison accuracy is governed by differences in approximation error across models rather than their absolute errors. More broadly, PC-LOO establishes posterior predictive simulation as a principled interface for integrating pretrained predictive learners into Bayesian workflows.

entry.title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Electric Vehicle Charging in a Time-varying Hierarchical Infrastructure

link.title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Electric Vehicle Charging in a Time-varying Hierarchical Infrastructure

entry.content:
Uncertainty quantification for electric vehicle (EV) charging demand is essential to turn the increasing pressure of EV adoption on power systems into a source of flexibility. We study a large-scale dataset of public charging stations in Scotland, where demand exhibits a hierarchical structure, organized across multiple aggregation levels, from individual charging points to regional and national scales. The charging infrastructure is continuously evolving, with new stations deployed and existing ones occasionally removed, which calls for forecasting and uncertainty quantification methods tailored to this evolving structure. To address these challenges, we combine hierarchical forecasting with recent advances in conformal prediction with missing data. The conformal procedures considered produce valid prediction intervals at every node of the hierarchy and the algorithm CP-MNR-Nested successfully accounts for the time-varying hierarchical structure of the data.

entry.title: Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities

link.title: Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities

entry.content:
Aggregating independently computed sub-sample inferences is a well-known challenge in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, and opinion pooling. The core problem is to approximate a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. We propose Product Monte Carlo (PMC), an algorithm for computing arbitrary expectations under a product of densities using only Monte Carlo draws from individual densities. We turn the intractable product expectation into a regression problem by expressing it through a family of computable conditional expectations. Besides the point estimate, our fully Bayesian regression formulation provides coherent uncertainty quantification and principled diagnostics. We establish theoretical guarantees on consistency and characterize convergence rates for the PMC estimator. Across simulated and real-data experiments varying the number, dimensionality, and heterogeneity of the component distributions, PMC achieves higher estimation accuracy, better-calibrated uncertainty coverage, and improved scalability at a lower computational cost than existing methods. In addition, PMC requires no density evaluation, making it applicable to simulation-based inference, as we demonstrate in an application with protein images.

entry.title: Provable Parameter-Free Fixed-Point Algorithms with Linear Convergence Rates

link.title: Provable Parameter-Free Fixed-Point Algorithms with Linear Convergence Rates

entry.content:
In this paper, we develop provable parameter-free fixed-point algorithms for contractive mappings, with an emphasis on automatically exploiting hidden contractivity without requiring prior knowledge of the contraction factor. Our first method is a parameter-free variant of the Halpern fixed-point iteration with no line-search, bisection, or prior estimate of the contraction factor, while retaining essentially the same per-iteration computational cost as classical fixed-point schemes. We establish explicit linear convergence rates for both the fixed-point residual and the distance to the unique fixed point. The second algorithm is also a parameter-free Halpern method, but it requires a line-search procedure to find a local estimate for the contraction factor, which may need a few additional operator evaluations. This method also enjoys explicit linear convergence guarantees. We further extend these ideas in two directions. First, using the relation between Halpern iterations and Nesterov-type accelerated fixed-point schemes, we derive parameter-free Nesterov-type (three-term) variants that inherit linear convergence in the contractive setting. Second, by combining the proposed fixed-point schemes with Tikhonov regularization, we obtain new methods for solving cocoercive equations and establish an iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}({\epsilon^{-1}\log(\epsilon^{-1})})$ for computing an $\epsilon$-solution, provided that a valid lower bound on the cocoercivity constant is available. Numerical experiments on several examples demonstrate that the proposed algorithms are competitive with, and often outperform, existing adaptive fixed-point methods. In particular, the methods successfully exploit contractive behavior when it is present on the selected nonexpansive test problems.

entry.title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction

link.title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction

entry.content:
Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $\epsilon=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

entry.title: Realized Tail-Risk Conditional Autoregressive Expectile Models: Accurate and Stable Forecasting Performance

link.title: Realized Tail-Risk Conditional Autoregressive Expectile Models: Accurate and Stable Forecasting Performance

entry.content:
A realized tail-risk conditional autoregressive expectile (RTCARE) model is proposed for joint forecasting of value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). Realized tail measures such as the realized quantile and the realized ES, constructed from intraday high-frequency returns, are incorporated into the dynamics and measurement equations of the conditional expectile, allowing information about lower-tail risk to enter the forecasts. The parameters are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and we evaluate the resulting VaR-ES forecasts in numerical examples and in an empirical application using U.S. stock-return data. Across the considered tail levels, the RTCARE models deliver competitive and often superior forecasting performance relative to existing alternatives, with stable results across Monte Carlo replications and rolling forecast evaluations.

entry.title: Reliability-Targeted Simulation of Item Response Data: Solving the Inverse Design Problem

link.title: Reliability-Targeted Simulation of Item Response Data: Solving the Inverse Design Problem

entry.content:
Monte Carlo studies of item response theory (IRT) methods often leave the information level implicit in the choice of item parameters. Designs with the same sample size and test length can therefore represent quite different measurement conditions. We develop a calibration procedure that makes the information level an explicit design choice. The target is an information-based reliability index derived from population mean test information. Before generating responses, we solve for a common multiplier on item discriminations, keeping difficulties, test length and the reference population fixed. The R package IRTsimrel implements the procedure, allowing researchers to compare methods across chosen information levels or compare designs at a common target. In an item-level treatment-effect simulation, power increases across targets, while excess rejection from ignoring item-effect variation persists. These comparisons show how targeting helps distinguish findings that depend on the chosen information level from those that persist across the studied range.

entry.title: Robust LassoNet: Enhancing Feature Selection in Neural Networks via Robust Loss Functions

link.title: Robust LassoNet: Enhancing Feature Selection in Neural Networks via Robust Loss Functions

entry.content:
Feature selection in neural networks remains a challenging problem, particularly in the presence of noisy or contaminated data. LassoNet is a recent approach that addresses this issue by combining neural networks with hierarchical sparsity constraints, enabling simultaneous prediction and variable selection. However, its standard formulation relies on the mean squared error (MSE) loss, which is known to be highly sensitive to outliers. In this paper, we present Robust LassoNet, an extension of LassoNet that incorporates robust loss functions, such as Huber, Cauchy, Tukey’s bisquare, and Nonnegative Garrote, to mitigate the effect of extreme observations. The proposed approach preserves the original optimization framework while improving stability under data contamination. Through experiments on synthetic and real datasets, we show that robust LassoNet significantly improves both predictive performance and feature selection accuracy in the presence of outliers or heavy tailed noise, while maintaining comparable performance in clean settings. These results highlight the importance of robustness in neural network based feature selection and suggest practical guidelines for choosing appropriate loss functions.

entry.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts

link.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts

entry.content:
Robust machine learning for regulatory genomics is studied under biologically and technically induced distribution shifts. Deep convolutional and attention based models achieve strong in distribution performance on DNA regulatory sequence prediction tasks but are usually evaluated under i.i.d. assumptions, even though real applications involve cell type specific programs, evolutionary turnover, assay protocol changes, and sequencing artifacts. We introduce a robustness framework that combines a mechanistic simulation benchmark with real data analysis on a massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) dataset to quantify performance degradation, calibration failures, and uncertainty based reliability. In simulation, motif driven regulatory outputs are generated with cell type specific programs, PWM perturbations, GC bias, depth variation, batch effects, and heteroscedastic noise, and CNN, BiLSTM, and transformer models are evaluated. Models remain accurate and reasonably calibrated under mild GC content shifts but show higher error, severe variance miscalibration, and coverage collapse under motif effect rewiring and noise dominated regimes, revealing robustness gaps invisible to standard i.i.d. evaluation. Adding simple biological structural priors motif derived features in simulation and global GC content in MPRA improves in distribution error and yields consistent robustness gains under biologically meaningful genomic shifts, while providing only limited protection against strong assay noise. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction offers an additional safety layer that risk coverage analyses on simulated and MPRA data show that filtering low confidence inputs recovers low risk subsets, including under GC-based out-of-distribution conditions, although reliability gains diminish when noise dominates.

entry.title: SAT-sampling for statistical significance testing in sparse contingency tables

link.title: SAT-sampling for statistical significance testing in sparse contingency tables

entry.content:
Exact conditional tests for contingency tables require sampling from fibers with fixed margins. Classical Markov basis MCMC is general but often impractical: computing full Markov bases that connect all fibers of a given constraint matrix can be infeasible and the resulting chains may converge slowly, especially in sparse settings or in presence of structural zeros. We introduce a SAT-based alternative that encodes fibers as Boolean circuits which allows modern SAT samplers to generate tables randomly. We analyze the sampling bias that SAT samplers may introduce, provide diagnostics, and propose practical mitigation. We propose hybrid MCMC schemes that combine SAT proposals with local moves to ensure correct stationary distributions which do not necessarily require connectivity via local moves which is particularly beneficial in presence of structural zeros. Across benchmarks, including small and involved tables with many structural zeros where pure Markov-basis methods underperform, our methods deliver reliable conditional p-values and often outperform samplers that rely on precomputed Markov bases.

entry.title: SLICE: Sequential Likelihood-Free Inference via Conformal E-Values

link.title: SLICE: Sequential Likelihood-Free Inference via Conformal E-Values

entry.content:
Many scientific models can be simulated but have intractable likelihoods, making frequentist uncertainty quantification difficult. We construct exact anytime-valid confidence sequences for the parameters of such models. At each observation, fresh simulations from each candidate null conformalize a positive predictable score into a conditional e-value; their product is a test martingale, which we invert over the parameter. Validity holds for any such score, whatever its accuracy. We show that the oracle likelihood-ratio score maximizes expected log growth, which motivates approximating it with an amortized neural ratio estimator. On synthetic benchmarks, an audit of model routing in an LLM API, and microlensing data, the resulting confidence sequences stay valid under continuous monitoring, where fixed-sample methods do not, and neural scores remain competitive with exact likelihood ratios and application-specific scores.

entry.title: SURF: Steering the Scalarization Weight to Uniformly Traverse the Pareto Front

link.title: SURF: Steering the Scalarization Weight to Uniformly Traverse the Pareto Front

entry.content:
Scalarization is widely used in multi-objective optimization owing to its simplicity and scalability. In many applications, the goal is to generate solutions that represent diverse user preferences, ideally with uniform coverage of the Pareto front (PF). However, uniformly sampling scalarization weights usually induces non-uniform coverage of the PF. We explain this mismatch through the geometry of the scalarization path. As the weight varies, the corresponding solutions traverse the PF at a generally nonuniform speed. Integrating this speed gives cumulative arc length. After normalization by the total length, it defines a cumulative distribution function (CDF) on weights whose inverse selects points at equal arc-length intervals. Building on this insight, we propose SURF (Sampling Uniformly along the Pareto Front). For structured problems, including bi-objective bandits, we derive analytical expressions for this CDF map and the resulting PF-aware weight sampling rule. For general problems, SURF alternates between CDF reconstruction and weight sampling. Theoretically, we show that under provable conditions for bi-objective LS, SURF’s CDF reconstruction error converges linearly to an $O(N^{-2})$ discretization floor. Empirically, experiments on bandits, multi-objective-gymnasium, and multi-objective LLM alignment demonstrate that SURF efficiently achieves more uniform PF coverage than baselines.

entry.title: Scalable Learning of Determinantal Point Processes with Kernel-Structured Interactions

link.title: Scalable Learning of Determinantal Point Processes with Kernel-Structured Interactions

entry.content:
Determinantal point processes (DPPs) on a finite set are probability models that exhibit repulsion where inter-item similarities are encoded by a positive definite kernel matrix. Scaling DPP learning to large datasets typically requires imposing structural constraints on the kernel matrix, such as a low-rank-plus-diagonal form. However, structural assumptions introduce a severe trade-off between expressive power and computational scalability. Our study addresses this challenge by (a) modeling the full-rank interactions via a nonlinear kernel function and latent features, (b) designing a surrogate function for the maximum likelihood estimator, and (c) adopting stochastic optimization using random features of the nonlinear kernel. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves this trade-off, achieving better generalization performance with remarkable parameter efficiency.

entry.title: Scalable Nonparametric Change-Plane Regression with Random Features: Estimation and Inference

link.title: Scalable Nonparametric Change-Plane Regression with Random Features: Estimation and Inference

entry.content:
Threshold and change-plane models provide a useful framework for capturing regime-dependent dynamics, but most existing approaches typically rely on scalar thresholds or linear splitting boundaries. We propose a scalable semiparametric change-plane regression framework that allows the regime boundary to depend nonlinearly on multivariate state variables. Random Fourier features provide a flexible and computationally efficient approximation to the nonlinear boundary function. A two-stage procedure first estimates the induced regime classification using a smooth surrogate and then refits the structural parameters by hard-threshold OLS. We establish convergence of the first-stage regime classification and show that its estimation error is asymptotically negligible for the second-stage refit, yielding oracle equivalence. We further develop a dependent-multiplier bootstrap Sup-Wald test for detecting the existence of regime effects when the boundary is unidentified under the null, and establish its asymptotic validity. Simulations demonstrate accurate regime recovery, near-oracle performance of the proposed estimator, and satisfactory finite-sample behavior of the Sup-Wald test. An application to postwar U.S. unemployment data provides strong evidence of regime dependence, while the estimated nonlinear change plane identifies a distinct stress regime characterized by significant shifts in short-run unemployment dynamics.

link.title: Scalable Sparse Autoregressive Variational Inference for Non-Gaussian Spatial Fields

entry.title: Scan-Parallel Variational Inference for event-driven Latent Jump Models

link.title: Scan-Parallel Variational Inference for event-driven Latent Jump Models

entry.content:
Continuous-time latent state-space models are widely used for irregularly observed time series, typically representing uncertainty through a random initial state followed by smooth ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics, or Brownian perturbations accumulated by a stochastic differential equation (SDE). While these constructions are natural for smooth or diffusive systems, they do not directly encode a finite set of unobserved shocks whose timing, magnitude, and effect on memory are themselves uncertain. We instead introduce latent jump models (LJMs): the latent state follows closed-form deterministic dynamics between Poisson-driven event times and undergoes a learned instantaneous jump at each event, with state-dependent intensity and mark distributions. This defines a time-homogeneous Markov process whose jumps are intrinsic state transitions rather than numerical integration steps. For training, we derive a tractable event-augmented path-space evidence lower bound (ELBO) and introduce Scan-Parallel Variational Inference (SPVI): an observation-conditioned variational posterior samples the complete latent event configuration before the state recurrence is evaluated using triangular affine scans. This enables fast and scalable training for LJMs in logarithmic temporal depth. Across synthetic stochastic systems and real irregular time series, LJMs remain competitive with continuous-time latent baselines in forecast accuracy, often with fewer latent updates than numerical solver evaluations, while training one to two orders of magnitude faster than the sequential baselines.

entry.title: Semiparametric Regression Based on Zero Altered Models

link.title: Semiparametric Regression Based on Zero Altered Models

entry.content:
We develop a class of semiparametric zero-altered models (ZAMs) for count data, estimated through the generalized method of moments (GMM). The proposed framework extends the utility of ZAMs by allowing for both under- and over-dispersion while preserving support on the entire set of natural numbers. This offers an alternative to other models that can experience computational challenges (e.g. Conway-Maxwell-Poisson) or whose supports can be truncated as functions of the parameter space (e.g. generalized Poisson). By formulating estimation through moment restrictions rather than full likelihood specification, the GMM approach provides substantial robustness against model misspecification. In particular, inference based on likelihood methods for parametric generalized linear models (GLMs), such as those built on Poisson, negative binomial, or related count distributions, can become unreliable when the assumed distributional form is violated, often leading to biased estimates and invalid inference. In contrast, our methodology requires only the first two moments of the distribution, ensuring consistent estimation even when higher-order distributional features are misspecified. We establish the asymptotic properties of the estimators, including consistency and asymptotic normality, under general regularity conditions. The flexibility of the approach is illustrated through both simulated experiments and real-data case studies, demonstrating superior performance relative to popular parametric GLMs, particularly in settings characterized by distributional misspecification. To facilitate practical adoption, we provide accompanying R functions for easy implementation, enabling practitioners to apply the proposed methods in applied settings without requiring bespoke programming.

entry.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection

link.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection

entry.content:
Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

entry.title: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs

link.title: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs

entry.content:
We develop standard errors for estimates of causal effects in settings where the distribution of treatment exposures is known but potentially exhibits complicated dependence patterns across units. Such dependence arises, for example, in settings with spillovers/interference across units or when the treatment assignment is spatially correlated. Our variance estimator generalizes several properties of the Neyman variance estimator for completely randomized experiments to general designs: it is unbiased for an upper bound on the variance from the design-based perspective; the conservativeness of this upper bound depends on the heterogeneity of treatment effects; and it is also valid under certain forms of super-population sampling of the potential outcomes. Our estimator reduces to standard approaches in simple designs, such as the Neyman variance estimator in completely randomized experiments and the cluster-robust variance estimator in cluster-randomized experiments. We show that the proposed estimator is admissible among the class of quadratic-form variance estimators, and derive asymptotic conditions under which it is consistent for an upper bound on the asymptotic variance of the treatment effect estimator. In simulations and applications based on two empirical studies, one with peer effects and another with a spatially correlated treatment, we find that the proposed variance estimator performs well, and in some cases yields standard errors that are 2-3 times shorter than those of existing alternatives.

entry.title: Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport

link.title: Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport

entry.content:
We discuss three simple connections between generative diffusion and optimal transport. First, the joint law of the data and of their Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noising is, at every time, the solution of an entropic optimal-transport problem, at a temperature set by the noise level. Backward diffusion can consequently be read as an annealing which gradually decreases the entropic regularization. Second, we study the speciation transition–how the modes of the data distribution emerge during generation–and compare how it happens in diffusion and flow matching with respect to optimal transport. Using Gaussian mixtures as high-dimensional example, we show that the dynamical instability through which diffusion and flow matching separate the modes becomes, for optimal transport, an exponentially thin boundary layer at the beginning of generation, which is rounded by entropic regularization. Third, considering a generic forward dynamics with a general confining potential, we show that the backward process driven by the score also satisfies a drift-based variational principle whose minimal cost is the entropy difference between initial and final distributions.

entry.title: Sparse Dictionary Learning for Measure-Valued Data via Linearized Optimal Transport: Efficient Algorithms and Sample Complexity

link.title: Sparse Dictionary Learning for Measure-Valued Data via Linearized Optimal Transport: Efficient Algorithms and Sample Complexity

entry.content:
We study dictionary learning for probability measure-valued data by embedding measures into Hilbert spaces using features derived from optimal transport geometry. We learn data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations, producing fast, scalable representations of probability measures as sparse finite-dimensional codes. The resulting framework combines the rich, geometric structure of optimal transport with the interpretability and efficiency of sparse representation learning. We demonstrate its utility across diverse data modalities, including hyperspectral images, geometric point clouds, and document embeddings in large language model latent spaces. We also prove generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning objectives on broad classes of $L^2$-valued measure embeddings, expressed in terms of the metric complexity of the atom class. For optimal transport and entropic transport map dictionaries, we derive new covering number bounds that yield explicit rates. Together, our computational and theoretical results support a new, scalable model for representation learning in the space of probability measures via embedding into Hilbert spaces.

entry.title: Spatial Prediction with Guided Diffusion

link.title: Spatial Prediction with Guided Diffusion

entry.content:
Spatial prediction is a critically important task in data analyses that involve spatially or spatio-temporally-referenced data. It is commonly carried out using hierarchical models, which comprise a process model describing the latent process of interest, and a data model describing how the process is observed. The target quantity is the predictive distribution, which is the conditional distribution of the latent spatial process given the observed data. Unfortunately, the predictive distribution is rarely available in closed form and can be difficult to sample from. Here, we show how recent developments in guided diffusion modelling from machine learning can address a wide class of problems in spatial prediction when the likelihood function derived from the data model is known and differentiable, possibly after relaxation. To show the versatility of the approach, we apply it to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian process models and a variety of data models that describe direct partial observations, linear and areal aggregates, counts, right censoring, and area-exceedance functionals. Where possible, we validate the framework against exact and Markov-chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC)-derived predictive distributions. We demonstrate our approach on several simulation studies and in a controlled experiment of methane-flux inversion over the UK and Ireland. We show that guided diffusion can sample from the correct predictive distribution in a variety of settings, that it can be applied to models where MCMC is intractable, and that it scales well with the dimensionality of the latent process.

entry.title: Surrogate Graph Partitioning for Spatial Prediction

link.title: Surrogate Graph Partitioning for Spatial Prediction

entry.content:
Spatial prediction refers to the estimation of unobserved values from spatially distributed observations. Although recent advances have improved the capacity to model diverse observation types, adoption in practice remains limited in industries that demand interpretability. To mitigate this gap, surrogate models that explain black-box predictors provide a promising path toward interpretable decision making. In this study, we propose a graph partitioning problem to construct spatial segments that minimize the sum of within-segment variances of individual predictions. The assignment of data points to segments can be formulated as a mixed-integer quadratic programming problem. While this formulation potentially enables the identification of exact segments, its computational complexity becomes prohibitive as the number of data points increases. Motivated by this challenge, we develop an approximation scheme that leverages the structural properties of graph partitioning. Experimental results demonstrate the computational efficiency of this approximation in identifying spatial segments.

entry.title: Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images with Conformal Uncertainty Estimation

link.title: Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images with Conformal Uncertainty Estimation

entry.content:
Thyroid nodules affect a large proportion of the general population. Although most are benign, a non-negligible fraction is malignant. Ultrasound imaging is the primary diagnostic modality, and accurate nodule segmentation is a prerequisite for CAD systems to classify malignancy and assess metastatic risk.\ In this work, we propose a thyroid nodule segmentation framework that integrates a DeepLabV3+, channel-attention modules and post-hoc conformal prediction, providing both accurate mask and pixel-level uncertainty estimates. We address thyroid ultrasound nodule segmentation as the first stage of a pipeline that also includes malignancy classification and metastatic risk prediction. We adopt DeepLabV3+, whose Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) captures multi-scale context, with an EfficientNet-B5 backbone for its accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Additionally, we test three channel-attention modules: Squeeze-and-Excitation, CBAM and Grouped Channel Attention (GCA), paired with two loss formulations (Dice-BCE and Boundary).\ Since binary masks do not indicate prediction confidence, we wrap the trained model with a split conformal prediction layer that produces pixel-level uncertainty maps with statistical coverage guarantees.\ We evaluate all configurations on the TN3K public benchmark using a fixed split and directly compare them with state-of-the-art methods. The plain backbone already improves upon previously reported results, with CBAM + Dice-BCE emerging as the best overall configuration.

entry.title: Transformer-Based Masked Diffusion Models Provably Learn Distributions with Latent Structure

link.title: Transformer-Based Masked Diffusion Models Provably Learn Distributions with Latent Structure

entry.content:
Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively unmasking multiple tokens in parallel using a learned mask predictor. Their output carries two errors: parallelization error due to parallel sampling, and estimation error from the mask predictor learned with finite samples. Existing theory treats these errors separately, and the available statistical bounds typically scale with the number $V^L$ of length-$L$ sequences over a vocabulary of size $V$, suffering from the curse of dimensionality. In this work, we establish end-to-end statistical guarantees showing that transformer-based MDMs learn structured distributions with a sample complexity governed by their latent structure. Specifically, we model this structure through mixtures of hidden Markov trees, which capture latent dependencies within components and heterogeneity across components. When the data distribution is well approximated by such a mixture, a transformer-based MDM with parallel unmasking schedules achieves $\varepsilon$-accurate sampling in KL divergence with $\widetilde{O}(LK_{\mathrm{par}}/\varepsilon)$ training samples, where $K_{\mathrm{par}}$ is polynomial in $L$, $V$, the number of hidden states, and the number of mixture components. The transformer network and sampling procedure require no knowledge of the tree topologies or component parameters, thereby adapting to the unknown latent structure automatically. Overall, our results provide theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of MDMs on real-world data.

entry.title: Two-way Guidance: Simultaneous Learning of Summary Statistics for Generative Bayes

link.title: Two-way Guidance: Simultaneous Learning of Summary Statistics for Generative Bayes

entry.content:
Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) can struggle to recover increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows. We consider learning sufficient summary statistics jointly with the posterior as a general principle for scalable inference in various SBI methods. A common measure taken in SBI is dimension reduction through predetermined summaries, which may partially discard posterior information. Our approach instead imposes structure on how the posterior learner depends on a learned summary (e.g., affinity), and learns the summary simultaneously with the posterior. We identify an important mechanism named two-way guidance: under a structural restriction on the summary, the posterior sufficiency of the learned summary simplifies posterior learning, whereas a suitable posterior objective guides the learned summary towards posterior sufficiency. This mechanism explains a counterintuitive finding that the structural restriction on the summary statistics improves posterior learning, rather than limit its performance. We establish theoretical guarantees on both posterior estimation error and the learned summary’s departure from sufficiency, thus identifying conditions on the simulation budget for recovering increasingly concentrated posteriors as observation size grows.

entry.title: TypedBench: A Benchmark for Calibration, Framing Sensitivity, and Cost in System One Decision Models

link.title: TypedBench: A Benchmark for Calibration, Framing Sensitivity, and Cost in System One Decision Models

entry.content:
System One models output calibrated probabilities over typed answers such as categorical choices, ordinal levels, or binary outcomes, via a non-generative interface. Software can act on these probabilities through thresholds, cost-weighted choices, and escalation rules. Consequently, if these probabilities are miscalibrated or wording-sensitive, the software ma take unintended actions leaving human operators with no textual rationale to inspect. Current evaluations largely report accuracy and calibration on public classification datasets without a clear reference. We present TypedBench, a benchmark for typed decision models like Jev built from seven policy-labelled generators and nine evaluation suites. We report accuracy as median and range across paraphrases, and calibration error relative to the finite-sample noise floor of a matched, perfectly calibrated predictor. We assess probability quality through selective prediction, ordinal proper scoring rules, and realised cost under asymmetric cost matrices. We evaluate a hosted model, an open encoder, and a family of open decoders spanning 0.8B-9B parameters on identical items. The hosted model follows the stated policy but is wording-sensitive and systematically underconfident; under asymmetric costs, using its probabilities can be worse than taking its top answer. Decoders route exactly and are slow as options or questions are added. The decoder is least accurate on policy questions and degrades with more options. Overall, typed decision models must be evaluated jointly on policy adherence, wording robustness, probability quality, and induced decision outcomes.

entry.title: Typical Healthcare Pathways as a Basis for Admixture Modeling of Patient Trajectories

link.title: Typical Healthcare Pathways as a Basis for Admixture Modeling of Patient Trajectories

entry.content:
Background: Understanding whether patients follow similar or distinct patterns of care is important for characterizing clinical practice, identifying patient subgroups, and supporting quality improvement. However, routine healthcare trajectories are difficult to compare directly because patients may differ in their diagnostic workup, treatment sequencing, timing of clinical events, and documentation practices. Despite this variation, trajectories often contain recurring patterns at the cohort level. Methods: To address this challenge, we present a framework that explicitly separates cohort-level typical pathway identification from patient-level inference. At the cohort level, we derive an interpretable representation of care processes using a rule-based algorithm to identify typical healthcare pathways, resulting in a compact pathway graph. These pathways are then modeled as Markov chains and used as structured components in an admixture model, allowing each patient to be represented as a probabilistic mixture of typical pathways rather than being assigned to a single pathway component. The resulting admixture weights provide a compact representation of patient trajectories for subgroup characterization. We further assess the stability of the identified pathways and inferred admixture representations across multiple train-test splits. Results: Across train-test splits, the framework demonstrated consistent pathway structures and patient-level mixture patterns. Applied to routine care data from prostate cancer patients undergoing radical prostatectomy, the framework identified interpretable care patterns and supported the identification of patient subgroups with similar clinical event patterns. Conclusion: Overall, the proposed framework provides an interpretable and stable approach for summarizing treatment pathways and characterizing patient subgroups in real-world practice.

link.title: Unsupervised Identification and Removal of Spurious Correlations During Fine-Tuning

entry.content:
Fine-tuning a pretrained language model on a curated dataset can produce spurious correlations between the fine-tuning task and unintended latent factors—such as misaligned personas or political slant—that the curation procedure has entangled with the task. The model can latch onto these spurious correlations, leading to bias and reduced out-of-distribution generalisation. We prove that under reasonable assumptions on task complexity and the spurious correlation, such latent factors can be identified, without supervision, from the weights of a naive LoRA fine-tune. Existing approaches to removing bias, such as activation steering, remove identified factors from residual-stream activations, either at inference or during training. We argue, however, that the goal should be to remove the spurious correlation, not the latent factor itself, as the pretrained model may rely on it for genuine task signal. To enable this, we propose GRASP, GRadient projection of Associated Spurious Patterns, which prevents the model from acquiring new reliance on the identified latent factor while preserving any pretrained content along it. We validate on three fine-tuning tasks. The first two involve emergent misalignment, where fine-tuning on a narrow task—in our case, writing insecure code and giving bad medical advice—leads to misaligned responses on unrelated topics. Here our method completely removes misalignment in the insecure code case and reduces it by ~5x in the bad medical advice case, beating all baselines in the trade-off between misalignment-reduction and task-preservation. The last is a novel political-bias experiment, where fine-tuning on right-skewed Reddit financial-advice data causes political-lean drift on unrelated topics. Here our method reduces drift by more than half, while improving financial task performance, beating all baselines.

entry.title: Warning of infrastructure deformation anomaly through probabilistic analysis of InSAR observations

link.title: Warning of infrastructure deformation anomaly through probabilistic analysis of InSAR observations

entry.content:
Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). We introduced a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements were modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function was defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance was evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings were identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework was validated using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

A limit state function was defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance was evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings were identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework was validated using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

entry.title: Where should the null live? Surrogate tests for clustering of threshold-derived air-quality indices, with application to PM2.5 exceedances in Chile

link.title: Where should the null live? Surrogate tests for clustering of threshold-derived air-quality indices, with application to PM2.5 exceedances in Chile

entry.content:
Air-quality and climate monitoring routinely convert native-resolution measurements into exceedance counts before testing whether high values cluster in time. A surrogate null can be imposed on the derived index or on the native series and then propagated through the same thresholding and aggregation. We show that the two placements can encode different scientific hypotheses and lead to opposite conclusions. In 31 Chilean PM2.5 monitoring stations (2018–2025), weekly clustering of days above the 50 ug m^-3 national 24-hour standard was significant at all stations under an index-level IAAFT null but at only two under a daily native-resolution null; a native generative null with seasonal marginals and short-memory Gaussian-copula dependence agreed with the native surrogate at 30 of 31 stations. Across thresholds spanning the WHO guideline (15 ug m^-3) to the Chilean episode-alert level (80 ug m^-3), index-only rejections increased from 8 of 31 to all eligible stations as monthly event probabilities became more seasonally concentrated, and equalizing monthly event probabilities at the 50 ug m^-3 level reduced index-only decisions from 29 to five. We formalize the issue as null transport through a lossy observation map: an exact aggregate-level equivalent of a native null exists if and only if the randomization kernel is lumpable with respect to that map. A within-fiber diagnostic, which perturbs native amplitudes while keeping the observed index exactly fixed, shows that this condition fails in the monitoring data: the native null distribution moved by a median of 18 times its Monte Carlo variability. Weekly clustering of PM2.5 exceedances in Chile is therefore fully compatible with seasonality plus short-memory daily persistence, and index-level surrogate rejections should not be read as evidence about daily concentration dynamics.

entry.title: Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality

link.title: Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality

entry.content:
A solid understanding of the predictive success of deep neural networks (DNNs) remains elusive. For example, while many data-dependent metrics exist that seek to predict model quality of DNNs, these metrics may be expensive to compute for large datasets and/or may be impossible to compute when training datasets are not released. A practical and effective predictor of model quality involves analyzing DNN weight matrices, as prior work has established that heavy-tailed spectral distributions in trained weight matrices can be strongly predictive of model quality. However, such metrics lack a rigorous statistical justification. In this work, we aim to understand why these metrics perform well, from a statistical perspective. To do so, we employ a probabilistic framework to derive the marginal likelihood for a DNN, evaluated using only the final layer weights. Across large-scale convolutional DNNs and LLMs, we find that this marginal likelihood predicts model quality. To understand the role heavy-tailed spectra play in predictive performance, we derive the limiting log-marginal likelihood for spectra that follow the (heavy-tailed) High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur (HTMP) distribution. We show that this limiting quantity is convex in a heaviness parameter, and we derive an optimal heaviness that empirically predicts over-fitting for large-scale DNNs.

entry.title: Work While They Sleep: Exploiting Evaluation Latency for Fully Bayesian Optimization

link.title: Work While They Sleep: Exploiting Evaluation Latency for Fully Bayesian Optimization

entry.content:
Black-box optimization problems are ubiquitous across science and engineering, often dealing with expensive objective functions. This objective latency has two consequences during optimization: (i) the objective evaluation dominates execution time, and (ii) sample-efficient algorithms are crucial to accelerate development and avoid wasting resources. Bayesian optimization (BO) methods are the \textit{de facto} choice of planners for suggesting the next point to try. Standard BO fits the surrogate model’s hyperparameters with a point estimate. Alternatively, a fully Bayesian approach uses model averaging to account for uncertainty over the hyperparameters, leading to better uncertainty estimates—useful in the low-data regime that is pervasive in BO. However, it is often prohibitively expensive and thus rarely used. In this work, we propose ELF-BO, an algorithm that uses the objective evaluation latency to headstart the computation of the next suggestion, allowing for fully Bayesian optimization without incurring substantial decision-time costs. This is done by sampling from the hyperparameter posterior \emph{while} the objective is being evaluated, only requiring reweighting of the samples once the objective value is observed. Across synthetic functions and real-world applications, we show that ELF-BO matches the performance of fully Bayesian methods while only incurring decision latency on par with or better than standard BO. Thus, ELF-BO makes fully Bayesian optimization practical in real-world use cases.

entry.title: bayprior: Structured Bayesian Prior Elicitation, Conflict Diagnostics, and Regulatory Reporting

link.title: bayprior: Structured Bayesian Prior Elicitation, Conflict Diagnostics, and Regulatory Reporting

entry.content:
Bayesian clinical trials require a well-specified prior distribution, and regulators increasingly expect that specification to be documented, diagnosed for prior-data conflict, and shown to be robust to reasonable alternatives, yet few R tools connect the full workflow of prior construction, validation, and regulatory justification into a single package. We introduce bayprior, an R package and Shiny application that implements structured expert elicitation via quantile matching, moment matching, and the SHELF roulette method across six distribution families; linear and logarithmic expert opinion pooling with Bhattacharyya agreement diagnostics; derivation of meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) priors from historical trial data via random-effects meta-analysis; prior-data conflict assessment using the Box p-value, S-value (surprisal) surprise index, information divergence, Bhattacharyya overlap, and multivariate Mahalanobis distance; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis with tornado and influence heatmap visualisations; and robust, sceptical, and power prior alternatives. A regulatory reporting module generates self-contained HTML, PDF, or Word documents addressing expectations in the FDA’s 2026 draft Bayesian methods guidance and in EMA guidance on incorporating external and historical information. The package is demonstrated on a synthetic oncology Phase II trial. bayprior is available on CRAN and includes a fully modular Shiny application for interactive use.

entry.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R

link.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R

entry.content:
Sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be before an observational conclusion changes. Established methods answer this question using different quantities, including partial $R^2$ values, correlation products, and risk ratios. In this article, we present confoundvis, an R package that organizes these results through a common object, plotting functions, and reports. It calculates partial $R^2$ and impact-threshold paths from fitted linear models, imports results from sensemakr, konfound, and EValue, and provides measured-covariate benchmarks for the OLS frameworks. We demonstrate the workflow with 5,735 patients from the right heart catheterization study. The adjusted linear probability coefficient is 0.0634, the point-null robustness value is 0.0608, and the conditional significance impact threshold is 0.0376. The largest adverse leave-one-term-out measured-covariate product is 0.0090. Because the benchmark and threshold use different conditioning sets, their ratio is descriptive. A separate modified Poisson model gives a risk ratio of 1.103 and an E-value of 1.439. The contribution is a software workflow that keeps each method’s units and decision rule clear. The package is available from CRAN.
